The bird shall be a 1.5 lb (0.68 kg) chicken, or an equivalent mass distribution, presented in a manner that simulates the most critical ingestion scenario. If, during this test, no bird material is ingested into the core, the test shall be repeated with the engine at the maximum takeoff power setting. If, under these conditions, no bird material is ingested into the core, the requirement is considered met. The test shall be conducted in accordance with the procedures specified in CS-E.60.11, ensuring that the bird is presented at the most critical angle of attack and that the engine is operating within its certified limits. The results of the test shall be documented, including the engine parameters, bird presentation details, and any observed effects on engine performance or structural integrity.

The engine manufacturer shall establish a procedure for the collection, identification, and recording of all debris released during a compressor or turbine blade failure test. For each test, the following data shall be recorded and documented in the test report: the total mass of the released debris, the mass of each individual fragment, and the physical dimensions of the largest fragment. Additionally, the material composition and the specific location of origin for each fragment shall be identified. The test report shall include a detailed description of the debris distribution, including the maximum distance traveled from the engine centerline and the specific engine components impacted by the debris. This documentation shall be maintained as part of the engine type design data package and shall be available for review by the Certification Authority. The recorded data shall be used to validate the containment analysis and to ensure that the engine meets the requirements of CS-E.1005, including the demonstration that no debris is released beyond the engine containment boundary or that any released debris does not pose a hazard to the aircraft structure or occupants.

The engine shall be capable of sustaining the maximum engine over-torque condition for a duration of at least 30 seconds. This requirement applies to engines equipped with a free power turbine where the over-torque condition is defined as a torque exceeding the maximum continuous torque rating. The test shall be conducted in accordance with the applicable test procedures, ensuring that the engine operates within its defined envelope of operation. The over-torque condition must be maintained without exceeding the limits specified in the engine's operating manual, including maximum gas generator speed and exhaust gas temperature. The 30-second duration is intended to verify the structural integrity and thermal stability of the engine components under transient high-torque loads, which may occur during rapid acceleration or specific operational scenarios. Compliance with this requirement shall be demonstrated through ground testing, and the results shall be documented in the engine's certification data package. The engine manufacturer shall provide evidence that the engine can safely operate under these conditions without degradation of performance or damage to critical components.

For engines with 30-Second/2-Minute OEI ratings, it must be shown that, following the loss of a single engine, the remaining engine(s) do not exceed the maximum continuous speed limit for more than 30 seconds. If the maximum continuous speed limit is exceeded, the engine must be capable of operating at the maximum continuous speed for the duration of the over-speed event without damage. The over-speed event is defined as the period during which the engine speed exceeds the maximum continuous speed limit. The demonstration must include the application of the maximum continuous power setting to the remaining engine(s) immediately after the failure. The engine must be capable of returning to the maximum continuous speed limit within 30 seconds of the over-speed event. The demonstration must be conducted under the most critical conditions, including maximum altitude and temperature, and with the engine at the maximum continuous power setting. The results of the demonstration must be documented in the engine manual, including the time to return to the maximum continuous speed limit and any limitations on the use of the engine following the over-speed event.

For the purpose of demonstrating rotor integrity, the engine shall be evaluated at the following speeds relative to the maximum permissible speed for the applicable rating:

(a) For normal ratings, the engine shall be evaluated at 100 percent of the maximum permissible speed.

(b) For OEI ratings of less than 2½ minutes, the engine shall be evaluated at 100 percent of the maximum permissible speed for the OEI rating. In addition, if the maximum permissible speed for the OEI rating is less than the maximum permissible speed for the normal rating, the engine shall also be evaluated at 100 percent of the maximum permissible speed for the normal rating.

The evaluation shall include consideration of the effects of any transient overspeed conditions that may occur during the transition from the OEI rating to the normal rating, or during the transition from the normal rating to the OEI rating, as applicable. The analysis shall demonstrate that the rotor system remains within its structural limits under these conditions, accounting for the specific torque and power characteristics associated with each rating.

For the purpose of torsional fatigue evaluation, the oscillatory torque shall be superimposed on the steady-state torque. The minimum amplitude of the oscillatory torque shall be 10 percent of the steady-state torque at the rated power and rated speed. This oscillatory torque shall be applied at a frequency corresponding to the first torsional natural frequency of the shaft system, or at a frequency that produces the maximum stress amplitude, whichever is more critical. The evaluation shall consider the combined effects of the steady-state and oscillatory torques to determine the total stress range. The material properties used in the fatigue analysis shall be representative of the actual shaft material, including any heat treatment and surface finish conditions. The number of cycles to failure shall be determined using the appropriate S-N curve for the material, adjusted for mean stress effects. The design shall ensure that the shaft has a fatigue life of at least 1,000 hours at the rated power and speed, or a life corresponding to the engine's intended service life, whichever is greater.

The most critical turbine rotor temperatures resulting from cooling air supply failures shall be established by analysis, test, or a combination of both. The analysis shall account for the maximum credible reduction in cooling air flow and the associated increase in turbine inlet temperature. Failures of the cooling air supply system that are shown to be extremely improbable, or that are mitigated by other independent systems, may be excluded from the determination of the most critical temperature. However, any failure that could result in a turbine rotor temperature exceeding the maximum allowable limit for the material in use, leading to loss of structural integrity or unacceptable performance degradation, shall be considered. The determination shall include the effects of transient conditions, such as engine start, acceleration, and deceleration, as well as steady-state operation at maximum continuous power. The results of this determination shall be used to define the limits for the engine's operating envelope and to ensure that the turbine rotor remains within its design temperature limits under all credible failure conditions.

The Maximum Exhaust Gas Over-temperature limit must be established by running the engine at the maximum exhaust gas temperature for a continuous period of 30 minutes. This run may be split into two or more periods, provided that the total duration of the run is at least 30 minutes and that the engine is operated at the maximum exhaust gas temperature for at least 10 minutes in each period. The engine must be operated at the maximum exhaust gas temperature for the entire duration of each period, and the engine must be allowed to cool to ambient temperature between periods. The maximum exhaust gas temperature is the highest temperature that the engine can sustain for the specified duration without exceeding the limits specified in CS-E.1005.

For engines utilizing refrigerant injection to restore ISA take-off performance at elevated ambient temperatures, the endurance test shall be conducted in accordance with CS-E.105, with specific modifications to the test conditions. The test shall be performed at the maximum ambient temperature for which the engine is certified, ensuring that the refrigerant injection system is operational and functioning within its specified limits. The engine shall be operated at the take-off power setting, with the refrigerant flow rate adjusted to maintain the required thrust or power output equivalent to ISA conditions. The endurance test duration shall be extended to include a minimum of 10 hours of continuous operation at this condition, or as specified by the engine manufacturer, to verify the long-term reliability of the refrigerant injection system and its associated components. During this period, the engine shall be monitored for any degradation in performance, abnormal vibrations, or leaks in the refrigerant system. The test shall be considered successful if the engine maintains the required performance parameters and no significant defects are identified in the refrigerant injection system or the engine itself.

For the purpose of demonstrating compliance with the structural and functional requirements of CS-E.60.10, the duration of use for thrust reverser systems shall be defined based on the specific operational profile. For ground-only reversers, which are utilized exclusively for post-landing braking and taxiing, a cumulative usage duration of 1,000 hours is assumed for the design life assessment. This duration accounts for the high-cycle fatigue and thermal stresses associated with repeated deployment and stowage cycles on the ground. Conversely, for thrust reversers designed for in-flight use, a cumulative usage duration of 10,000 hours is assumed. This extended duration reflects the continuous operational environment and the additional aerodynamic and mechanical loads experienced during flight. The applicant shall demonstrate that the thrust reverser system, including all associated actuators, control mechanisms, and structural components, retains its required performance and safety margins throughout these specified durations. The assessment shall include consideration of the maximum number of cycles expected within these timeframes, ensuring that no degradation in function or structural integrity occurs that would compromise the safe operation of the engine or the aircraft.

The propeller parking brake shall be operated a minimum of 100 times during the endurance test. Each operation shall consist of applying the brake while the propeller is rotating at a speed not less than 1,000 rpm, and releasing the brake while the propeller is rotating at a speed not less than 1,000 rpm. The brake shall be applied and released in a manner representative of normal operating conditions. The endurance test shall include a minimum of 100 cycles of brake application and release, with the propeller speed maintained at or above 1,000 rpm during both the application and release phases. The test shall be conducted under conditions that simulate the most severe expected operational environment, including temperature and altitude variations. The results of the endurance test shall demonstrate that the parking brake system maintains its functional integrity and performance characteristics throughout the specified number of cycles, with no degradation in braking efficiency or mechanical reliability.

For the purposes of the turbine over-temperature test, the term "maximum power-on rotor speed" refers to the highest rotor speed attained during the test condition, excluding any transient speeds resulting from the application of the maximum power-on setting. This value is typically the steady-state rotor speed corresponding to the maximum power-on condition as defined in the engine specification. However, if the engine exhibits a transient rotor speed that exceeds the steady-state maximum power-on rotor speed due to the dynamics of the power-on transient, this transient speed shall be used for the test. The transient rotor speed is the peak speed reached during the transient period following the application of the maximum power-on setting, before the engine settles to its steady-state operating point. The test must be conducted at this transient speed to ensure that the turbine is subjected to the most severe thermal and mechanical conditions that could occur in service. The use of the transient speed is critical for accurately assessing the turbine's ability to withstand the maximum thermal loads without exceeding the allowable temperature limits.

The engine test required to substantiate the initial maintenance programme (IMP) must simulate the most severe operating conditions expected to be encountered in service. This includes, but is not limited to, the maximum continuous power or thrust rating, the maximum take-off power or thrust rating, and the maximum continuous temperature limits. The test shall also include a representative cycle of start, idle, acceleration, cruise, and deceleration, as well as a period of operation at the maximum continuous power or thrust rating. The test duration shall be sufficient to demonstrate that the engine meets the reliability and maintainability requirements of CS-E.1455. The test shall be conducted in accordance with the test procedures specified in the engine type design data. The results of the test shall be documented and made available to the authority for review. The test shall be repeated if any significant changes are made to the engine design or the maintenance programme.

The operational design specifications for turbine engines are established to define the specific operating limits and procedures necessary to ensure the safe and reliable operation of the engine. These specifications serve as the primary reference for the operator, detailing the maximum and minimum values for parameters such as engine pressure ratio, exhaust gas temperature, and rotational speed, as well as the permissible ranges for ambient conditions. By clearly delineating these boundaries, the specifications prevent the engine from being operated in regimes that could lead to structural failure, performance degradation, or hazardous conditions. Furthermore, they provide the basis for the development of the engine’s operating manual and the associated maintenance procedures, ensuring that all personnel involved in the operation and upkeep of the engine are aware of the critical parameters that must be monitored and controlled. The purpose is ultimately to maintain the engine within its certified envelope, thereby preserving the integrity of the propulsion system and ensuring compliance with the safety objectives of the certification specification.

For time-limited dispatch with faults in an Electronic Engine Control System, the time-weighted average of the full-up and dispatch configurations must meet the rate of 10⁻⁷ per engine flight hour. This requirement ensures that the probability of a hazardous failure due to the fault condition remains within acceptable limits for the duration of the dispatch. The calculation of this rate shall consider the specific fault modes and their associated probabilities, as well as the operational profile of the engine. The time-weighted average is determined by integrating the failure rates over the expected operational time, taking into account the varying conditions under which the engine operates. This approach provides a robust method for assessing the safety of the engine under fault conditions, ensuring that the overall risk remains within the specified limits. The determination of this rate shall be documented and reviewed as part of the safety assessment process, ensuring compliance with the applicable certification requirements.

CS-E 1040.1 requires that the engine be designed to provide the thrust required for the applicable ETOPS flight time. The engine must be capable of operating at the required thrust level for the duration of the ETOPS flight time without exceeding the limits specified in the engine type certificate data sheet. The engine must also be designed to ensure that the probability of an in-flight shutdown (IFSD) is less than 1.0 x 10^-5 per flight hour. This requirement is intended to ensure that the engine can reliably provide the necessary thrust for the extended range operation, thereby maintaining the safety and reliability of the aircraft during ETOPS flights. The engine manufacturer must demonstrate compliance with this requirement through analysis, testing, or a combination of both, as appropriate. The demonstration must include a detailed assessment of the engine's reliability and the probability of an IFSD, taking into account the specific operating conditions and maintenance procedures associated with ETOPS operations.

AMC CS-E.1005 Volcanic Clouds

1. The following turbine engine features may be susceptible to airworthiness effects from volcanic clouds:

a) Turbine engine hot sections, including combustors, turbine blades, and turbine disks, which may experience accelerated erosion, corrosion, or thermal degradation due to the ingestion of volcanic ash particles.

b) Engine fuel systems, including fuel nozzles, fuel lines, and fuel pumps, which may become contaminated or clogged by volcanic ash, leading to uneven fuel distribution or fuel flow interruptions.

c) Engine air intake systems, including inlet guide vanes and compressor stages, which may suffer from foreign object damage (FOD) or increased wear due to the abrasive nature of volcanic ash particles.

d) Engine control systems, including sensors and actuators, which may experience malfunction or reduced accuracy due to the presence of volcanic ash in the engine environment.

e) Engine exhaust systems, including exhaust nozzles and afterburners, which may experience increased wear or damage due to the high-temperature and abrasive nature of volcanic ash.

2. The applicant shall identify and evaluate the potential airworthiness effects of volcanic cloud ingestion on these features, and shall implement appropriate design, operational, or maintenance measures to mitigate these effects.

AMC CS-E 34.11-1

The expansion space of the hydraulic fluid reservoir should be designed to accommodate the maximum anticipated increase in fluid volume due to thermal expansion and system pressure variations. For engine-mounted reservoirs, the expansion space is recommended to be at least 10 percent of the total reservoir capacity. This margin ensures that the fluid level remains within the operational limits of the reservoir during all certified flight conditions, including maximum ambient temperature and maximum engine power settings. The reservoir design should also account for the compressibility of the fluid and the potential for air entrainment. The expansion space should be clearly marked or indicated to facilitate maintenance and inspection. The adequacy of the expansion space should be verified through analysis or testing, demonstrating that the fluid level does not exceed the maximum allowable level under any certified operating condition. The reservoir should be designed to prevent fluid spillage in the event of a leak or overfilling. The expansion space should be considered in the overall system design to ensure that the hydraulic system operates within its specified parameters.

The APU shall be capable of starting under the conditions specified in CS-E1.13. During the endurance test, the APU shall complete a minimum of 100 successful starts. These starts shall be distributed throughout the test duration to simulate typical operational profiles, including cold starts, hot starts, and starts following a period of operation. Each start shall be considered successful if the APU reaches its rated speed and provides the required electrical and pneumatic power within the time limits specified in the applicable data sheet. The test shall include starts from a cold condition, where the APU has been shut down for a minimum of 30 minutes, and from a hot condition, where the APU has been operating at full power for a minimum of 10 minutes prior to shutdown. The results of these starts shall be recorded and analyzed to ensure that the APU meets the reliability and performance requirements of CS-E1.13. Any failed start shall be investigated, and corrective actions shall be taken to ensure that the APU can reliably start under all specified conditions.

CS-E 11.15.1: The main rotor brake must be operated at least 100 times during the engine endurance test. The brake must be applied and released in a manner representative of normal helicopter operation, including application during forward flight at the maximum rated speed and during hover. Each application must be sufficient to stop the rotor system within the time specified in the helicopter type certificate data sheet. The brake must be inspected after the 50th and 100th applications to verify that no damage, excessive wear, or degradation of performance has occurred. If any such condition is found, the brake must be repaired or replaced, and the endurance test must be continued until the total number of operations reaches 100. The results of these inspections must be recorded in the test report. This requirement ensures that the brake system maintains its integrity and performance throughout the life of the engine, particularly under the thermal and mechanical stresses encountered during prolonged operation.

For engines intended for use in turbine-powered airplanes approved for extended-range operations, the applicant shall demonstrate that the in-flight shutdown (IFSD) rate is less than 0.30 per 1,000 engine hours. This requirement applies to engines installed in airplanes approved for 180-minute ETOPS operations. The IFSD rate shall be determined based on the engine’s operational history, including data from the engine’s type certification basis and subsequent service experience. The applicant must provide evidence that the engine design, maintenance procedures, and operational limitations collectively ensure that the probability of an in-flight shutdown due to engine failure or malfunction remains below the specified threshold. This demonstration shall account for all relevant failure modes, including those associated with fuel system, ignition system, and structural components. The data used for this calculation must be representative of the engine’s expected service environment and shall be reviewed and approved by the competent authority.

For the purpose of demonstrating compliance with CS-E.10.15, the fuel contamination rate for piston engines tested with sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) blends shall be determined in accordance with the applicable ASTM standard for the specific blend ratio. When testing with SAF blends, the contamination level shall not exceed the limits specified for the corresponding petroleum-based fuel reference standard, adjusted for the specific properties of the bio-component. The test fuel shall be prepared to contain a maximum of 0.005 percent by volume of water and 0.005 percent by volume of particulate matter, unless a higher limit is explicitly justified by the engine manufacturer and accepted by the Agency. The measurement of these contaminants shall be performed using the methods outlined in ASTM D2708 for water and sediment, and ASTM D5200 for particulate matter, ensuring that the sampling procedure accounts for the potential phase separation characteristics of the SAF blend. Compliance is demonstrated if the engine operates within the specified performance and emissions limits under these defined contamination conditions.

CS-E.115.15 requires that the engine be capable of being restarted in flight. The flight crew must be able to unlock the engine rotor-locking device, if fitted, within a time not exceeding 10 seconds. This requirement ensures that the engine can be brought to a condition suitable for ignition and subsequent acceleration to idle speed within the time limits specified for engine restart. The unlocking mechanism must be operable by the flight crew from the cockpit, and the time interval is measured from the initiation of the unlock command to the point where the rotor is free to rotate. This provision is critical for maintaining engine availability during flight, particularly in scenarios where an engine has been shut down and needs to be restarted for continued operation or for emergency procedures. The 10-second limit is designed to balance the need for rapid engine availability with the practical constraints of mechanical and hydraulic systems used in rotor-locking devices.

CS-E 10.15(a) requires that the engine be designed to operate within specified limits. For glycol-cooled piston engines, the maximum permissible coolant temperature is 100 °C. This limit is established to ensure the integrity of the cooling system components, including hoses, seals, and the radiator, under normal operating conditions. The engine manufacturer must demonstrate compliance with this temperature limit through ground and flight testing, as outlined in AMC 10.15-1. The testing procedure shall verify that the coolant temperature does not exceed 100 °C when the engine is operating at maximum continuous power in the hottest ambient conditions for which the engine is certified. If the engine is equipped with a temperature control system, such as a thermostat or an electric fan, the system must be shown to maintain the coolant temperature at or below this limit. Exceeding this temperature may result in coolant boiling, loss of lubrication, or damage to the engine block and cylinder heads. The certification authority will review the test data to confirm that the 100 °C limit is not exceeded under any normal operating condition, including high-altitude and high-temperature scenarios.

The methods of compliance for the requirements of this Specification, other than those contained in the second volume of these Rules, may be established by the use of other acceptable means of compliance. Specifically, the European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) may accept other methods of compliance that are demonstrated to be acceptable. Furthermore, the requirements of this Specification may be met by the use of other acceptable means of compliance, including those contained in other EASA publications, such as the Engine Certification Specifications (CS-E) for specific engine types, or other applicable standards and guidelines, provided that the applicant demonstrates that the proposed method of compliance is acceptable to the Agency. The applicant shall submit a detailed description of the proposed method of compliance, including any supporting data, for review and approval by the Agency. The Agency may require additional data or testing to verify the acceptability of the proposed method of compliance.

AMC CS-E 14.10-1

The applicant may demonstrate compliance with the requirements of CS-E 14.10 by providing a detailed analysis of the engine’s structural integrity under the specified load conditions. This analysis shall include a description of the test procedures, the criteria for acceptance, and the results of any applicable tests. The applicant is encouraged to refer to the Advisory Material (AM) associated with CS-E 14.10, which provides additional guidance on acceptable means of compliance. Furthermore, the applicant may consult the EASA Certification Specifications for Engines (CS-E) Amendment 9, Book 2, which contains detailed methods and techniques for demonstrating compliance with the requirements of Book 1. In cases where the specific requirements of CS-E 14.10 are not fully addressed in Book 2, the applicant may also refer to the EASA Technical Specifications for Engines (TS-E) or other relevant EASA documents that provide accepted compliance methods. The applicant shall ensure that all compliance methods are documented and that the results are traceable to the applicable requirements.

CS-E.100 Applicability. This Part applies to the certification of gas turbine engines and powerplants. For the purposes of this Part, a "powerplant" is defined as the engine, its accessories, and the associated fuel, oil, and air systems, including the exhaust system, as installed in the aircraft. The requirements of this Part are applicable to all gas turbine engines and powerplants, regardless of their intended use, whether for propulsion or for the generation of electrical or mechanical power. Where a powerplant is certified for use in an aircraft, the specific installation requirements of CS-25 or CS-23, as applicable, shall also be met. The certification basis for a gas turbine powerplant shall include the applicable requirements of CS-E, including the structural, performance, and safety provisions, as well as any additional requirements specified by the competent authority. The provisions of this Part are mandatory for the issuance of a type certificate for a gas turbine engine or powerplant.

CS-E 00.05 Applicability. This Part applies to the certification of gas turbine engines, including those intended for use in aircraft, helicopters, and unmanned aircraft systems. The applicant shall comply with the requirements of CS-E 00.05 through CS-E 33.05, as applicable to the specific engine type and its intended operating conditions. For engines certified under this Part, compliance with the following chapters is mandatory: CS-E 00 (General), CS-E 01 (Definitions), CS-E 02 (Certification), CS-E 03 (Engine Design), CS-E 04 (Engine Performance), CS-E 05 (Engine Reliability), CS-E 06 (Engine Maintenance), CS-E 07 (Engine Installation), CS-E 08 (Engine Testing), CS-E 09 (Engine Data), CS-E 10 (Engine Marking), CS-E 11 (Engine Records), CS-E 12 (Engine Reporting), CS-E 13 (Engine Safety), CS-E 14 (Engine Environment), CS-E 15 (Engine Noise), CS-E 16 (Engine Emissions), CS-E 17 (Engine Fuel), CS-E 18 (Engine Oil), CS-E 19 (Engine Cooling), CS-E 20 (Engine Ignition), CS-E 21 (Engine Starting), CS-E 22 (Engine Control), CS-E 23 (Engine Monitoring), CS-E 24 (Engine Protection), CS-E 25 (Engine Vibration), CS-E 26 (Engine Fatigue), CS-E 27 (Engine Fracture), CS-E 28 (Engine Corrosion), CS-E 29 (Engine Wear), CS-E 30 (Engine Aging), CS-E 31 (Engine Degradation), CS-E 32 (Engine Failure), CS-E

The term "damage tolerance" refers to the capability of a structure to sustain a specified level of damage, such as a crack or impact, without catastrophic failure, and to remain safe for a defined period of time. This concept is fundamental to the design of safety-critical powerplant hardware, ensuring that the structure can withstand the effects of fatigue, corrosion, and accidental damage. The design must demonstrate that the structure can tolerate the growth of a flaw from an initial detectable size to a critical size, which is the size at which failure would occur, within the established inspection interval. This is achieved through a combination of material selection, design features that limit crack propagation, and a rigorous inspection program. The objective is to ensure that the probability of failure due to damage is acceptably low, thereby maintaining the integrity of the engine and the safety of the aircraft. The damage tolerance approach is a key element of the airworthiness requirements, ensuring that the powerplant can operate safely throughout its service life.

The term "damage tolerance" refers to the ability of a structure to sustain a specified level of damage without catastrophic failure, provided that the damage is detected and the structure is repaired or replaced before further damage accumulates. In the context of CS-E, this concept is applied to critical parts where failure could lead to engine failure or loss of the aircraft. The design must ensure that any single failure of a critical part does not result in a hazardous condition. This is achieved by demonstrating that the part can withstand the expected damage mechanisms, such as fatigue, corrosion, or impact, over its service life. The analysis must consider the probability of damage occurrence and the consequences of that damage. If a part is identified as critical, the design must incorporate features that allow for the detection of damage, such as through visual inspection or non-destructive testing, and must provide for the repair or replacement of the part before the damage reaches a critical level. The objective is to ensure that the engine remains safe and reliable throughout its operational life, even in the presence of undetected or unexpected damage.

The airframe provides the electronic powerplant controller with data such as airspeed, altitude, and engine operating parameters, as well as power supply and communication interfaces. The airframe manufacturer must define the specific data requirements, including format, update rate, and accuracy, that the electronic powerplant controller requires from these airframe-provided sources. This definition must be established through the interface control document, ensuring that the airframe supplies the necessary information in a manner that allows the electronic powerplant controller to perform its functions safely and reliably. The airframe manufacturer is responsible for verifying that the provided data meets the specified requirements, while the engine manufacturer must ensure that the electronic powerplant controller is designed to utilize this data correctly. Both parties must coordinate to resolve any discrepancies and ensure compatibility between the airframe and the electronic powerplant controller, thereby maintaining the integrity of the overall system.

AMC CS-E.10.10(b)

1. The Engine and Engine Installation Interface (EEI) document shall define the specific requirements for all items supplied by the aircraft to the Engine and Engine Control System (EECS). This includes, but is not limited to, electrical power, pneumatic air, hydraulic fluid, fuel, and data signals.

2. The engine manufacturer is responsible for identifying the specific characteristics of these supplied items that are critical to the safe operation of the EECS. These characteristics may include voltage levels, frequency, pressure ranges, flow rates, temperature limits, and signal formats.

3. The EEI document shall clearly state the acceptable ranges and tolerances for each supplied item. For example, if the EECS relies on aircraft-supplied electrical power, the document shall specify the minimum and maximum voltage, the acceptable frequency range, and the required power quality. Similarly, for pneumatic air, the document shall define the minimum and maximum pressure and temperature.

4. The aircraft manufacturer shall ensure that the supplied items meet the requirements defined in the EEI document. The engine manufacturer shall verify that the EECS functions correctly within the specified ranges of the supplied items.

5. Any changes to the supplied items that could affect the EECS performance shall be evaluated by both the engine and aircraft manufacturers to ensure continued compliance with the applicable certification specifications.

The maintenance manual shall contain detailed instructions for routine servicing, including the frequency, procedures, and criteria for determining the condition of the powerplant. These instructions shall be sufficient to enable the operator to maintain the powerplant in a condition that complies with the applicable airworthiness requirements. The manual shall specify the intervals for routine servicing, which may be expressed in terms of time, cycles, or other appropriate parameters, and shall include the specific tasks to be performed at each interval. The procedures shall be clear, unambiguous, and shall include all necessary steps, tools, and materials required. The manual shall also provide guidance on the interpretation of results and the actions to be taken if the powerplant does not meet the specified criteria. The information shall be presented in a logical sequence, with cross-references to other sections of the manual as necessary. The manual shall be updated to reflect any changes in the powerplant design, maintenance procedures, or applicable regulations.

The engine manufacturer shall provide instructions for the servicing of the engine. These instructions shall include, but are not limited to, the following:

(a) A description of the servicing tasks, including the frequency and the specific conditions under which they are to be performed.
(b) The tools, equipment, and materials required to perform the servicing tasks, including any special tools or test equipment.
(c) The safety precautions and warnings necessary to prevent injury to personnel or damage to the engine.
(d) The procedures for checking and adjusting engine parameters, such as fuel flow, oil pressure, and temperature, to ensure the engine operates within its certified limits.
(e) The procedures for inspecting, cleaning, and lubricating engine components, including the removal and replacement of filters and seals.
(f) The procedures for recording servicing data, including the date, time, and results of each servicing task, in the engine maintenance records.
(g) The procedures for reporting any discrepancies or defects discovered during servicing to the appropriate authority.

The instructions shall be written in a clear and concise manner, using standard aviation terminology and units of measurement. They shall be readily accessible to the maintenance personnel and shall be updated as necessary to reflect any changes in the engine design or operating procedures.

The applicant shall demonstrate that the lubrication system design accounts for the specific installation environment, including the orientation of the engine within the aircraft structure. The analysis must consider the effects of aircraft maneuvers, including positive and negative accelerations, pitch, roll, and yaw, on the oil supply and return lines. It shall be established that the oil level in the sump remains within the operational limits required to maintain adequate lubrication and cooling of all engine components under all anticipated flight conditions. This includes verification that the oil supply to the bearings and gears is not interrupted by cavitation or air ingestion during transient maneuvers. The design shall ensure that the oil return system prevents oil accumulation in areas where it could cause fire hazards or interfere with other aircraft systems. Furthermore, the applicant shall demonstrate that the lubrication system maintains the required oil pressure and flow rate throughout the engine operating envelope, including during start-up, idle, and maximum power conditions, while accounting for the temperature variations expected in the installation.

The engine installation shall provide for the supply of lubricating oil to the engine and the return of used oil to the aircraft oil system. The oil system shall be designed to ensure that the engine is supplied with oil at the required pressure and temperature throughout the range of operating conditions. The oil tank capacity shall be sufficient to allow for the engine to operate for the maximum continuous time specified in the engine manual without refilling, taking into account any oil consumption during the take-off and landing phases. The oil system shall include provisions for the measurement of oil quantity and pressure, and for the indication of low oil pressure to the pilot. The oil return system shall be designed to prevent the accumulation of oil in areas where it could pose a fire hazard. The oil system shall be designed to prevent the ingress of foreign matter into the engine. The oil system shall be designed to allow for the easy inspection and maintenance of the oil system components. The oil system shall be designed to allow for the easy replacement of the oil filter. The oil system shall be designed to allow for the easy replacement of the oil pump.

For rotorcraft equipped with multiple powerplants, the engine output levels for use in the event of a powerplant failure shall be established to ensure the aircraft can meet the applicable performance requirements. The engine manufacturer shall provide the following output levels for use in the event of a powerplant failure:

a) A continuous output level, which the engine is capable of maintaining for an unlimited period of time; and

b) A time-limited output level, which the engine is capable of maintaining for a specified period of time, not exceeding 30 minutes, to allow for the safe completion of the flight or the safe landing of the aircraft.

The time-limited output level shall be clearly identified in the engine operating manual, and the associated time limitation shall be indicated on the engine indication system. The engine shall be designed to ensure that the time-limited output level does not result in damage to the engine or its components when operated within the specified time limit. The engine manufacturer shall provide data to support the determination of these output levels, including the effects of ambient temperature, pressure altitude, and other relevant operating conditions.

For turbine engines installed in multi-engine rotorcraft, the applicant may apply for the following Out-of-Envelope (OEI) ratings, as defined in CS-E.10:

1.  **OEI-1**: The engine is capable of producing the rated power for a continuous period of 30 minutes, followed by a 2-minute period at 110 percent of the rated power.
2.  **OEI-2**: The engine is capable of producing the rated power for a continuous period of 5 minutes, followed by a 2-minute period at 110 percent of the rated power.
3.  **OEI-3**: The engine is capable of producing the rated power for a continuous period of 2 minutes, followed by a 2-minute period at 110 percent of the rated power.

The specific OEI rating applied for must be consistent with the rotorcraft’s operational requirements and the engine’s design limitations. The applicant must demonstrate compliance with the applicable time limits and power levels through testing or analysis, ensuring that the engine can sustain the required output without exceeding the maximum allowable turbine inlet temperature or other critical parameters. The selection of the OEI rating should be clearly stated in the engine’s type certificate data sheet and reflected in the rotorcraft’s flight manual.

The 30-second OEI setting shall be engaged and regulated by a self-acting system to ensure the powerplant operates within its certified limits during the critical 30-second period following an engine failure. Manual engagement by the person flying the aircraft is prohibited because it introduces unacceptable human factors risks, including delayed reaction time, potential for incorrect selection, and distraction from immediate flight control tasks. A self-acting system guarantees that the required fuel flow, fuel pressure, and ignition conditions are established and maintained automatically, without reliance on pilot memory or manual intervention. This ensures consistent and reliable engine performance, allowing the pilot to focus on the emergency procedure and the safe landing of the aircraft. The system must be designed to prevent inadvertent disengagement and to provide clear indication of its status. This requirement is essential to maintain the safety margin necessary for a successful autorotation and landing within the 30-second OEI time limit, as defined in CS-E.2605.

AMC CS-E.10.10: To ensure the reliability and repeatability of the engine-out (OEI) performance demonstration, the test procedure shall be executed automatically by a dedicated test system rather than by manual pilot input. This requirement addresses the inherent variability in human reaction times and control inputs, which can introduce significant uncertainty into the measured parameters. By automating the initiation of the OEI condition, the test ensures that the engine is shut down at a precisely defined point in the flight envelope, typically at a specific rotor RPM or power setting, with a consistent time delay of 30 seconds. This 30-second interval is critical to allow the engine to spool down to a defined residual speed, ensuring that the subsequent performance data reflects a stable, worst-case scenario for the rotorcraft’s ability to maintain controlled flight. Manual execution risks premature or delayed engine shutdown, potentially masking performance deficiencies or creating non-representative data. Therefore, an automated system is necessary to guarantee that the OEI performance is demonstrated under consistent, repeatable conditions that accurately reflect the engine’s actual capability during an in-flight failure, thereby ensuring the safety margins required for certification are valid and verifiable.

AMC CS-E 33.15-1

The requirement for a gauge to monitor the turbine heat removal system may be waived if the engine design incorporates a redundant, independent monitoring system that provides continuous indication of the heat removal fluid flow or temperature to the flight crew. This alternative system must be designed to meet the reliability standards specified in CS-E 33.15 and must provide an immediate, unambiguous warning to the flight crew in the event of a failure or degradation of the heat removal system. The warning must be distinct from other engine warnings and must be clearly identifiable as relating to the turbine heat removal system. The engine manufacturer must demonstrate, through analysis and testing, that the alternative monitoring system provides an equivalent level of safety and reliability to the required gauge. The demonstration must include a failure mode analysis that identifies all single and multiple failures of the monitoring system and shows that no single failure can result in a loss of indication without a warning. The results of this analysis must be documented in the engine certification data package and made available to the flight crew through the engine operating manual.

CS-E 33.13 Turbine cooling system.

(a) The turbine cooling system shall be designed to ensure that the turbine cooling air flow is adequate to prevent damage to the turbine components under all operating conditions.

(b) If the turbine cooling system is not monitored by a dedicated instrument that provides continuous indication of cooling air flow or temperature to the flight crew, the engine shall be designed such that:

(1) The cooling system is fail-safe, ensuring that any failure results in a condition that does not lead to immediate engine damage or loss of thrust; or

(2) The engine is equipped with a monitoring system that detects abnormal cooling conditions and provides a warning to the flight crew, allowing for corrective action or engine shutdown before damage occurs.

AMC CS-E 33.13 Turbine cooling system.

One acceptable means of compliance is to provide a dedicated turbine cooling air flow indicator or a turbine inlet temperature indicator that alerts the crew to potential cooling deficiencies. Alternatively, if the cooling system is designed to be inherently safe against failure, such as through redundant cooling paths or automatic shut-off valves that close upon loss of pressure, a dedicated continuous monitoring instrument may not be required, provided that the design analysis demonstrates that no single failure can lead to turbine damage.

Forged powerplant parts shall be sorted into three grades based on the extent of internal and surface imperfections detected during non-destructive inspection. Grade 1 parts are those that exhibit no internal or surface imperfections exceeding the limits specified in the applicable material specification. These parts are suitable for use in critical structural components where high fatigue resistance and reliability are required. Grade 2 parts contain minor imperfections that do not compromise the structural integrity of the part but may limit its application to less critical areas. Grade 3 parts contain imperfections that exceed the limits for Grade 2 and are generally rejected or used only for non-critical applications where the imperfections do not affect performance. The classification of parts into these grades shall be documented in the quality control records, and the acceptance criteria for each grade shall be clearly defined in the applicable material specification.

AMC CS-E.10.10

(1) For apparatus fitted to the powerplant that contains rotating members capable of storing significant kinetic energy, compliance with the requirements of CS-E.10.10 may be demonstrated by one of the following means:

(a) The rotating members are designed such that, in the event of a failure, the stored energy is dissipated within a time interval that does not result in hazardous conditions to the aircraft or its occupants. This may be achieved through the use of energy-absorbing materials or mechanical damping mechanisms that limit the release of energy to levels that are not hazardous.

(b) The rotating members are protected by a containment system that is designed to withstand the maximum expected energy release from a failure of the rotating members. The containment system shall be designed to prevent the ejection of fragments that could cause hazardous conditions. The design shall be verified by analysis, testing, or both, demonstrating that the containment system can withstand the maximum expected energy release without failure.

(c) The rotating members are designed such that the energy stored in them is limited to a level that is not hazardous in the event of a failure. This may be achieved by limiting the rotational speed or the mass of the rotating members. The design shall be verified by analysis, demonstrating that the maximum stored energy is below the threshold for hazardous conditions.

(2) The selection of the appropriate means of compliance shall be based on a risk assessment that considers the likelihood and severity of potential failures, as well as the consequences of such failures to the aircraft and its occupants.

CS-E.10.10 requires that the engine be designed to prevent the release of hazardous debris from the engine in the event of a failure. For equipment containing high-energy rotors, such as accessory drives or starter generators, the applicant may demonstrate compliance with the requirements of CS-E.10.10 by one of the following means:

(a) The equipment is designed such that a failure of the rotor or its support structure will not result in the release of debris that could damage the engine or the aircraft structure, or injure personnel on the ground.

(b) The equipment is protected by a containment system that is designed to withstand the energy of a rotor failure without rupture, thereby preventing the ejection of hazardous fragments.

(c) The equipment is located in a position such that any released debris will not strike critical engine components, the aircraft structure, or personnel on the ground, as determined by a detailed analysis of the debris trajectory and energy.

The applicant shall provide evidence, such as analysis, test data, or a combination thereof, to demonstrate that the selected method ensures that the probability of a hazardous debris release is negligible, and that any released debris is contained or directed away from critical areas.

AMC CS-E.10.10: To guard a powerplant from corroding, the use of non-corrosive substances is required whenever feasible. Where the use of non-corrosive substances is not feasible, the use of corrosive substances shall be limited to the minimum extent necessary, and the powerplant shall be designed to prevent the accumulation of such substances in areas where they could cause damage. The selection of materials and the design of the powerplant shall ensure that any corrosive substances used are contained or neutralized in a manner that prevents adverse effects on the structural integrity of the engine. The applicant shall demonstrate compliance with this requirement by providing a detailed analysis of the materials used and the potential for corrosion, including the results of any relevant testing. The analysis shall consider the operating environment, including exposure to moisture, chemicals, and temperature variations, and shall identify any areas of the powerplant that are particularly susceptible to corrosion. The applicant shall also provide a maintenance plan that includes procedures for inspecting and treating any areas of the powerplant that are at risk of corrosion.

AMC CS-E.10.10: To prevent corrosion, the engine manufacturer shall employ materials and surface treatments that provide adequate protection against the environmental conditions expected during the engine's service life. Where feasible, corrosion-resistant materials such as stainless steels, nickel-based alloys, or aluminum alloys with appropriate anodizing or chemical conversion coatings shall be utilized for components exposed to moisture, salt spray, or chemical contaminants. For ferrous components where corrosion-resistant materials are not practicable, protective coatings such as zinc plating, cadmium plating, or organic coatings shall be applied in accordance with applicable industry standards. The selection of materials and coatings shall be documented in the engine's maintenance manual, specifying inspection intervals and reapplication criteria. Corrosion protection shall be verified through testing in accordance with CS-E.10.10(b), demonstrating that the protective system maintains its integrity under simulated operational and storage conditions. The manufacturer shall provide data demonstrating that the selected materials and coatings do not adversely affect the structural integrity, performance, or maintainability of the engine components.

AMC CS-E 33.15-1

The structural integrity of safety-critical components, such as the fan disk, compressor disks, and turbine disks, shall be evaluated considering not only the static strength limits of the material but also the effects of fatigue, creep, and low-cycle fatigue (LCF) under the expected operational duty cycle. The analysis shall account for the combined stresses arising from centrifugal forces, thermal gradients, and aerodynamic loads. Furthermore, the assessment must incorporate the impact of transient events, including engine start-up, shutdown, and rapid acceleration or deceleration, which induce significant thermal and mechanical shock. The margin of safety shall be determined by comparing the calculated stresses against the applicable material properties, adjusted for the specific temperature and time-dependent degradation mechanisms. The evaluation shall also consider the potential for crack initiation and propagation, ensuring that the component retains sufficient structural margin to prevent catastrophic failure throughout its certified life. The analysis shall be supported by test data where analytical methods are insufficient to demonstrate compliance with the required safety margins.

CS-E.3350 Turbine rotor and stator blades.

(a) The turbine rotor and stator blades shall be designed to withstand the maximum expected stresses, including those resulting from the combined effects of centrifugal, thermal, and aerodynamic loads, without exceeding the applicable material strength limits.

(b) In addition to the stress limits specified in paragraph (a), the design shall account for the effects of creep, fatigue, and low-cycle fatigue. The analysis shall consider the maximum operating temperature and the corresponding thermal gradients across the blade section.

(c) The design shall also allow for the effects of vibration, including resonance conditions, and the potential for foreign object damage (FOD) or erosion, where applicable. The margin of safety shall be demonstrated through analytical methods, validated by test data, or a combination thereof, in accordance with CS-E.3350(b).

AMC-E.3350(b)

The assessment of creep and fatigue life shall be based on the material properties at the maximum operating temperature. The analysis shall include the effects of thermal cycling and the associated thermal stresses. The vibration analysis shall identify critical speeds and ensure that the operating range avoids resonance conditions with adequate margins. The effects of FOD and erosion shall be evaluated based on the expected operational environment and the material's resistance to such damage mechanisms.

CS-E.1005(b) requires that the engine be designed to prevent the assembly of parts in a manner that would result in a hazardous engine effect. Where it is not possible to prevent such assembly by design, the engine shall be designed to ensure that the hazardous effect is not initiated by the incorrect assembly. Acceptable Means of Compliance (AMC) to CS-E.1005(b) include the use of positive mechanical features, such as keyed splines, asymmetric bolt patterns, or unique part numbers, that physically prevent the installation of incompatible components. Additionally, the engine maintenance documentation shall include explicit warnings and procedural checks to verify the correct orientation and identification of critical parts, such as turbine blades, disks, and shafts. The design shall ensure that any potential misalignment or incorrect mating of components does not lead to uncontained failure, excessive vibration, or loss of structural integrity during operation. Compliance with this requirement shall be demonstrated through design analysis, physical inspection of mating features, and review of the associated maintenance and assembly instructions to confirm that the risk of hazardous engine effects due to incorrect assembly is mitigated to an acceptable level.

CS-E 120.15 requires that the powerplant be marked in accordance with the provisions of Part 21, Subpart J, and Subpart K. Specifically, the marking must comply with the requirements of CS-E 120.15(a) through (d), which detail the permanent and legible identification of the powerplant, including the manufacturer’s name, model designation, serial number, and the date of manufacture. The marking must be located in a position that is readily accessible for inspection and must not be obscured by any other markings or components. Furthermore, the powerplant must be marked with the certification basis, including the applicable CS-E amendment level, to ensure traceability and compliance with the applicable airworthiness requirements. The marking must be durable and resistant to environmental conditions, ensuring that it remains legible throughout the service life of the powerplant.

The applicant shall identify the engine in accordance with the requirements of Part 21, Subpart A, and Subpart B. Specifically, the engine must be assigned a type designation in accordance with Article 21.15, which shall be unique and shall not be used for any other engine type. The type designation shall be clearly marked on the engine in a permanent and legible manner, in accordance with Article 21.16. Furthermore, each individual engine unit shall be assigned a serial number in accordance with Article 21.17. This serial number shall be unique to the specific engine and shall be permanently marked on the engine in a location that is readily accessible for inspection. The marking of the type designation and serial number shall be such that it cannot be removed or altered without obvious evidence of tampering. The applicant shall ensure that the identification markings are consistent with the data provided in the type design data package and the production data package, as required by CS-E 120. Compliance with these identification requirements is a prerequisite for the issuance of a type certificate and a production certificate under Part 21.

The fire-resistant label shall be affixed to components that demonstrate the ability to withstand a fire exposure for a duration of at least 30 seconds. This specific time interval is established to ensure that the component can maintain its structural integrity and prevent the propagation of flames to adjacent fuel, oil, or hydraulic lines during the critical initial phase of a fire event. The 30-second span is considered sensible because it aligns with the minimum time required for the engine fire detection system to reliably sense the fire and for the fire extinguishing agent to be discharged and begin suppressing the flame. By ensuring the component remains intact for this period, the design provides a sufficient margin for the fire suppression system to act effectively, thereby preventing the fire from escalating into a catastrophic engine failure or airframe damage. This requirement ensures that the fire-resistant material does not fail prematurely, allowing the engine to continue operating or shut down safely without the fire spreading beyond the engine compartment.

AMC CS-E 34.11-1: To demonstrate compliance with the fire resistance requirements of CS-E 34.11, the part shall be subjected to a fire test in which the part is exposed to a flame for a period of at least 30 seconds. This duration is considered sufficient to ensure that the part can withstand the thermal loads and potential ignition sources encountered during engine operation, including fuel leaks or oil sprays, without failing in a manner that would compromise the safety of the aircraft. The 30-second exposure time is based on the maximum expected duration of a fire event in the engine compartment, taking into account the time required for fire detection and suppression systems to activate and control the fire. Parts that fail to maintain their structural integrity or that allow the fire to spread beyond the protected area during this test period are not considered fire-resistant. The test conditions, including the type of fuel, flow rate, and temperature, shall be in accordance with the test procedures specified in the applicable test standard, such as SAE AS5089 or equivalent, to ensure consistent and reproducible results.

The bonding of powerplant pieces to their common ground point shall be designed to keep small the harm from built-up static or other stored-up electricity. This requirement ensures that any electrical potential differences between structural components, engine accessories, and the airframe are minimized, thereby preventing unintended electrical discharges, corrosion, or interference with sensitive avionics systems. The bonding network must provide a low-impedance path to safely dissipate static charges generated by fuel flow, air ingestion, or other operational factors. Acceptable means of compliance include the use of continuous conductive paths, such as metal-to-metal contact or dedicated bonding straps, that maintain electrical continuity throughout the service life of the engine. The design shall account for the accumulation of charge during normal and abnormal operating conditions, including high-altitude flight and exposure to lightning strikes. Regular inspection and maintenance procedures shall be established to verify the integrity of bonding connections, ensuring that resistance values remain within specified limits to maintain effective grounding.

The purpose of providing a low-impedance electrical path between engine components and the airframe ground is to minimize the risk of electrostatic discharge (ESD) and associated hazards. Specifically, this requirement is intended to keep to a minimum the following problems:

1.  **Ignition of flammable vapors:** High-voltage discharges can ignite fuel vapors or other flammable fluids in the vicinity of the engine.
2.  **Damage to sensitive electronic equipment:** Transient voltage spikes can disrupt or destroy avionics, engine control units, and other electronic systems.
3.  **Corrosion of electrical connections:** Poor grounding can lead to stray currents, causing accelerated corrosion at connection points and degrading the integrity of the electrical system.
4.  **Interference with communication and navigation systems:** Electrostatic discharge can generate electromagnetic interference (EMI), degrading the performance of critical aircraft systems.

Compliance with these requirements ensures that static charges are safely dissipated, thereby maintaining the safety and reliability of the engine and the aircraft as a whole.

AMC CS-E.10.10

1. During test runs of a gas turbine engine, if the ancillary take-offs on the power turbine carry no burden, the engine shall be operated in a manner that ensures the power turbine does not exceed its certified limits. Specifically, the engine control system shall be configured to prevent overspeed conditions of the power turbine. This may be achieved by:

a) Installing a dummy load or equivalent resistance on the ancillary take-offs to simulate the normal operating load; or

b) Utilizing an engine control system that automatically limits the fuel flow to the power turbine section to maintain the power turbine speed within its certified operational envelope, even when no external load is applied.

2. The test procedure shall document the method used to prevent power turbine overspeed and shall demonstrate compliance with the applicable speed limits specified in CS-E.10.10. The engine manufacturer shall provide evidence that the control system or dummy load arrangement effectively prevents the power turbine from exceeding its maximum certified speed during all test conditions where ancillary take-offs are unloaded.

AMC CS-E.10.10: To demonstrate compliance with the requirements of CS-E.10.10, the applicant shall conduct engine tests with the power turbine accessory drives unloaded. During these tests, the engine shall be operated at the maximum continuous power rating and at the maximum continuous speed. The test shall be conducted for a duration sufficient to demonstrate that the engine can operate within the specified limits without exceeding the maximum allowable temperatures or pressures. The test shall be conducted in accordance with the test procedures specified in the engine type certificate data sheet. The results of the test shall be recorded and reported to the Agency. The Agency shall review the test results and determine whether the engine complies with the requirements of CS-E.10.10. If the engine does not comply, the applicant shall take corrective action and repeat the test. The corrective action shall be documented and reported to the Agency. The Agency shall review the corrective action and determine whether the engine now complies with the requirements of CS-E.10.10.

AMC CS-E.105(b)

1. To ensure that the powerplant has reached a steady-state condition following a change in operating parameters, readings shall not be taken until the powerplant has been operated in the new condition for a sufficient duration.
2. For gas turbine engines, the stabilization time shall be determined by the engine manufacturer based on the specific engine design and the magnitude of the change in operating state. As a general guideline, a minimum stabilization time of 30 seconds is recommended for changes in thrust or power settings, provided that the engine parameters (e.g., EGT, N1, N2, fuel flow) have remained within a specified tolerance band (e.g., ±1% of the steady-state value) for the last 10 seconds of the stabilization period.
3. For piston engines, a minimum stabilization time of 2 minutes is recommended after any change in manifold pressure or propeller RPM, ensuring that oil temperature and pressure have stabilized within the limits specified in the engine manual.
4. The specific stabilization times and tolerance bands shall be documented in the engine test procedure and approved by the Agency.

The engine shall be operated at the specified test conditions for a sufficient duration to ensure that all relevant parameters have reached a steady state prior to data acquisition. For the purpose of performance validation, steady state is defined as the condition where the measured parameters remain within the specified tolerance limits for a continuous period. Unless otherwise specified in the applicable test procedure, the engine shall be held at the new operating condition for a minimum of 30 seconds, or until the indicated values stabilize within ±1 percent of the final reading, whichever is longer. Readings taken prior to the establishment of this steady state shall not be included in the performance data set. The test operator shall document the time required to reach steady state for each condition change. If the engine exhibits transient behavior that prevents stabilization within a reasonable timeframe, the test shall be aborted, and the cause investigated before resuming the test sequence.

The applicant shall submit a detailed report to the Agency within ten working days of the occurrence of any failure or malfunction during the qualification runs. This report shall include a complete description of the failure, the time of occurrence, the operating conditions, and the specific components affected. The applicant shall immediately cease the qualification runs and shall not resume them until the Agency has reviewed the failure analysis and approved the corrective actions. The applicant shall provide evidence that the root cause of the failure has been identified and that the necessary design, manufacturing, or maintenance changes have been implemented to prevent recurrence. If the failure indicates a potential safety hazard, the applicant shall notify the Agency of any other engines or components that may be affected. The Agency may require additional testing or analysis to verify that the corrective actions are effective and that the powerplant continues to meet the requirements of this Specification. The applicant shall maintain records of all failures, analyses, and corrective actions for a period of at least five years.

In the event of a failure or malfunction of any engine component or system during a certification test, the applicant shall immediately suspend the test and notify the Certification Authority. The applicant is required to conduct a detailed investigation to determine the root cause of the failure, including a physical examination of the failed component and a review of all relevant test data. A written report detailing the nature of the failure, the corrective actions taken, and the rationale for any subsequent test modifications shall be submitted to the Certification Authority. If the failure indicates a non-compliance with the applicable requirements of CS-E, the applicant shall implement necessary design or procedural changes to ensure compliance. The certification test shall be resumed only after the Certification Authority has reviewed and accepted the investigation report and any proposed corrective actions. The applicant shall ensure that all subsequent tests are conducted in accordance with the approved test plan, and any deviations from the original test conditions must be justified and approved by the Certification Authority prior to resumption of testing.

The applicant shall demonstrate that the High-Intensity Radiated Field (HIRF) and lightning protection system of the partial engine setup is representative of the full engine configuration. This demonstration shall be accomplished by providing a detailed engineering analysis that accounts for the electrical and physical differences between the tested partial setup and the complete engine. The analysis must verify that the current distribution, potential gradients, and thermal effects on critical components, such as the fan case, core cowl, and internal structures, are not adversely affected by the absence of the untested sections.

Where the partial setup omits specific structural elements, the applicant shall provide evidence that the omitted sections do not alter the primary current paths or create new points of high potential difference that could compromise the integrity of the lightning protection system. This may include finite element analysis (FEA) of the electrical network, comparison of measured current densities with predicted values, and verification of bonding resistance across all interfaces. The analysis shall confirm that the partial setup’s performance meets the requirements of CS-E.25.975 and CS-E.25.977, ensuring that the full engine will withstand the specified lightning strike conditions without catastrophic failure or loss of function.

CS-E 175.15 Propeller blade-angle regulating hardware.

The propeller blade-angle regulating hardware that is part of the approved powerplant configuration must meet the applicable requirements of CS-P 175.15, CS-P 175.17, CS-P 175.19, CS-P 175.21, CS-P 175.23, CS-P 175.25, CS-P 175.27, CS-P 175.29, CS-P 175.31, CS-P 175.33, CS-P 175.35, CS-P 175.37, CS-P 175.39, CS-P 175.41, CS-P 175.43, CS-P 175.45, CS-P 175.47, CS-P 175.49, CS-P 175.51, CS-P 175.53, CS-P 175.55, CS-P 175.57, CS-P 175.59, CS-P 175.61, CS-P 175.63, CS-P 175.65, CS-P 175.67, CS-P 175.69, CS-P 175.71, CS-P 175.73, CS-P 175.75, CS-P 175.77, CS-P 175.79, CS-P 175.81, CS-P 175.83, CS-P 175.85, CS

CS-E 175.1 requires that the propeller pitch control system, when part of the engine type design, comply with the applicable requirements of CS-P. Specifically, the following CS-P provisions apply to the pitch control system: CS-P 175.1 (General), CS-P 175.2 (Pitch Control System), CS-P 175.3 (Pitch Control System Design), CS-P 175.4 (Pitch Control System Performance), CS-P 175.5 (Pitch Control System Reliability), CS-P 175.6 (Pitch Control System Maintenance), CS-P 175.7 (Pitch Control System Inspection), CS-P 175.8 (Pitch Control System Testing), CS-P 175.9 (Pitch Control System Documentation), and CS-P 175.10 (Pitch Control System Certification). The applicant must demonstrate compliance with these requirements through analysis, test, or both, as appropriate. The pitch control system must be designed to ensure that the propeller blades remain in the desired pitch position under all anticipated operating conditions, including failure conditions. The system must also be designed to prevent unintended changes in propeller pitch that could result in hazardous conditions.

AMC CS-E.10.15(b)

The long qualification run shall include a minimum of three complete feathering sequences. Each sequence shall consist of the following actions:

1.  Reduce engine power to the minimum required to maintain the specified airspeed.
2.  Command the propeller to the feathered position.
3.  Verify that the propeller blades have reached the feathered position and that the propeller is locked in that position.
4.  Command the propeller to the normal operating position.
5.  Verify that the propeller blades have returned to the normal operating position and that the propeller is unlocked.

The feathering sequences shall be performed at the following conditions:

*   At the maximum continuous power setting.
*   At the minimum continuous power setting.
*   At the idle power setting.

The results of each feathering sequence shall be recorded and shall demonstrate that the propeller system operates in accordance with the requirements of CS-E.10.15.

AMC CS-E.10.15: To demonstrate compliance with the requirements for propeller feathering during engine failure, the applicant shall perform the following checks during the long endurance run. The propeller feathering system shall be exercised a minimum of three times. Each exercise shall consist of initiating the feathering command, allowing the propeller to reach the feathered position, and subsequently returning the propeller to the operating position. The time required for the propeller to reach the feathered position shall not exceed the limits specified in CS-E.10.15(b). The applicant shall record the time for each feathering cycle and verify that the propeller returns to the correct operating position without abnormal vibration or noise. These checks shall be conducted at the maximum continuous power setting and at the minimum continuous power setting, as applicable, to ensure the system functions correctly across the operating envelope. The results of these checks shall be documented in the test report and shall demonstrate that the feathering system operates reliably under the conditions specified in the certification basis.

The powerplant shall be shown to be capable of withstanding the maximum engine speed and the maximum engine pressure, as applicable, for the powerplant, without damage, and without exceeding the limits specified in CS-E.1005. For powerplants installed in fixed-wing aircraft for which the operating handbook permits aerobatic or semi-aerobatic manoeuvres, it shall be shown that the powerplant is capable of withstanding the maximum engine speed and the maximum engine pressure, as applicable, for the powerplant, without damage, and without exceeding the limits specified in CS-E.1005, under the conditions of the most severe aerobatic manoeuvre. The clearance for such manoeuvres shall be noted in the powerplant type certificate data sheet. The demonstration of compliance may be accomplished by test, analysis, or a combination thereof. The analysis shall be based on a detailed understanding of the powerplant’s response to the aerodynamic loads and inertial forces associated with the specified manoeuvres. The results of the demonstration shall be documented in the powerplant type certificate data sheet, indicating the specific aerobatic or semi-aerobatic manoeuvres for which the powerplant has been shown to be suitable.

The applicant shall demonstrate that the engine is suitable for the aerobatic or semi-aerobatic manoeuvres specified in the Aeroplane Flight Manual. This demonstration shall include verification that the engine can sustain the maximum continuous power output required for the specified manoeuvres without exceeding the limits established in CS-E.250. The applicant shall provide data showing that the engine operates within its approved envelope under the specific load factors and airspeeds associated with the manoeuvres. The approval shall be documented in the engine type certificate data sheet, explicitly stating the maximum continuous power rating and the specific aerobatic or semi-aerobatic manoeuvres for which the engine is approved. This statement shall be cross-referenced in the Aeroplane Flight Manual to ensure operational consistency. If the engine is not approved for a specific manoeuvre, the Aeroplane Flight Manual shall restrict the operation accordingly. The applicant shall submit a report detailing the test conditions, results, and any limitations imposed on the engine's operation during these manoeuvres to the Agency for review and inclusion in the certification record.

CS-E.1005(b) requires that the probability of a powerplant failure or malfunction that would result in a hazardous condition be less than 10^-4 per flight hour. For the purposes of this assessment, a hazardous condition is defined as one that could result in serious injury or death to some of the occupants.
