Where the engine is equipped with a full-authority digital engine control (FADEC) system, the applicant shall show that the control system prevents the engine from exceeding these limits under all anticipated operating and failure conditions. The demonstration shall include analysis and, where necessary, testing to verify that the engine’s safety margins are maintained. The applicant shall identify the specific operating limits and the methods used to ensure compliance, including the use of limit sensors and protective functions. The evidence shall be sufficient to show that the engine will not be damaged by any combination of operating conditions that could be encountered in service, including those resulting from plausible emergency situations.

The engine must be designed such that, under normal operating conditions and in the event of likely emergency situations, it does not exceed the limits specified in CS-E10.15. Specifically, the engine must demonstrate that it will not exceed the maximum allowable gas generator speed, turbine inlet temperature, or fuel flow limits that would result in structural failure or loss of thrust control. For each likely emergency condition, including fuel control system failures, the applicant must show by analysis, test, or both, that the engine remains within its certified operating envelope. If the engine is capable of exceeding these limits, the design must incorporate safeguards, such as overspeed protection or fuel flow limiting, to prevent damage. The demonstration must account for the worst-case combination of environmental conditions and engine operating parameters. The applicant must provide data showing that the engine can safely shut down or return to a stable operating condition without exceeding the structural limits of the engine components. This includes verifying that the engine does not experience uncontrolled acceleration or that the gas temperature does not exceed the material limits of the turbine blades.

The pilot shall be able to release the engine starter inhibitor switch, if provided, to permit the operation of the starter. The starter shall be capable of rotating the engine shafts to a speed sufficient to allow for a successful relight under the conditions specified in CS-E.1455. The starter shall be designed to prevent inadvertent operation during flight, except when the engine is in a condition requiring a relight. The pilot shall be able to monitor the starter operation and shall be provided with a means to stop the starter if it fails to engage or if the engine does not light within the specified time. The starter shall be capable of withstanding the maximum torque and temperature conditions encountered during a relight attempt. The pilot shall be able to identify the status of the starter and the engine ignition system through the cockpit instrumentation. The starter shall be designed to prevent damage to the engine or airframe in the event of a failure. The pilot shall be able to safely shut down the engine if a relight attempt is unsuccessful.

The rotor lock shall be designed such that it can be released from the cockpit during an air restart sequence. The release mechanism shall be operable by the flight crew without requiring the use of tools or access to the engine compartment. The design shall ensure that the rotor lock is fully disengaged and the rotor is free to rotate prior to the initiation of the air restart procedure. The pilot shall be able to verify the status of the rotor lock through a cockpit indication, which shall clearly display whether the lock is engaged or released. This indication shall be illuminated when the lock is engaged and shall extinguish upon successful release. The system shall be designed to prevent inadvertent engagement of the rotor lock during flight. In the event of a failure of the primary release system, an alternate means of release shall be provided, which shall be accessible to the flight crew and operable within a time frame consistent with the engine air restart procedure. The design shall account for the effects of vibration, temperature, and pressure on the reliability of the release mechanism.

The engine shall be subjected to a long-duration powerplant running test with the permanently-on firing arrangement in operation. This test shall be conducted at the maximum continuous power rating for a duration of at least 10 hours, or as specified in the engine type design data, to verify the stability of the combustion process and the absence of abnormal vibrations or temperature excursions. The test shall include a minimum of 100 start cycles, with each start initiated from a cold or hot condition, to demonstrate the reliability of the ignition system under representative operating conditions. During the test, the engine shall be operated through the full range of power settings, including idle, takeoff, and maximum continuous power, to ensure that the firing arrangement functions correctly across all operating regimes. The results of the test shall be recorded and evaluated to confirm that the engine meets the performance and durability requirements specified in CS-E.250 and CS-E.251.

The endurance run shall be conducted in accordance with the requirements of CS-E.100. The total duration of the endurance run shall be 1,000 hours of operation. This duration includes all time during which the engine is operating, regardless of the ignition system status. The requirement for the ignition system to be operational does not reduce the total required operating time. Therefore, the full 1,000 hours of engine operation must be accumulated. The time during which the always-on ignition system is active is included within this total 1,000-hour requirement. There is no separate, additional time requirement specifically for ignition system operation beyond the total endurance run duration. The engine must be operated for the full 1,000 hours, with the ignition system functioning as required by CS-E.100 and applicable sections of CS-E.33 and CS-E.34. The endurance run is not reduced by the time the ignition system is active; rather, the ignition system must be active for the entire duration of the 1,000-hour run if it is an always-on system. Thus, the remaining time owed is the difference between 1,000 hours and the hours already accumulated during the endurance run, with the ignition system active for all of that remaining time.

AMC CS-E.115(b)

The 30-second and 2-minute OEI settings are not required to satisfy the output reference-curve checks specified in CS-E.115(b)(1) because these settings are transient conditions intended solely for engine-out performance calculations. The output reference curve, defined in CS-E.115(b)(1), establishes the steady-state relationship between engine output and ambient conditions for normal operation. Since the 30-second and 2-minute OEI settings are time-limited and do not represent a steady-state operating point, applying the steady-state output reference curve checks would be inappropriate and potentially misleading. Instead, these transient settings are evaluated based on their specific time-limited power output capabilities, as defined in CS-E.115(b)(2) and (3), which account for the temporary nature of the engine-out condition. The regulatory intent is to ensure that the engine can provide the necessary thrust or power for a defined duration during an engine-out scenario, without requiring compliance with the steady-state performance characteristics that apply to continuous operation. This approach ensures that the certification process accurately reflects the operational reality of engine-out events, where the engine is operated at a higher power setting for a limited time to maintain aircraft performance.

AMC CS-E.115(b)

The 30-second and 2-minute OEI points are excluded from the standard turbine calibration runs because these specific operating conditions are not representative of the steady-state performance characteristics required for engine certification. The 30-second point is a transient condition used to verify the engine's ability to recover from a single engine failure, while the 2-minute point is a short-duration limit used for take-off thrust settings. These points are governed by specific time-limited power provisions and are not intended to define the engine's continuous or maximum continuous rating. Including them in the calibration process would introduce unnecessary variability and complexity, as the calibration is designed to establish the baseline performance for continuous operation. The 30-second and 2-minute OEI points are instead verified through separate, dedicated test procedures that focus on the engine's transient response and short-duration limits, ensuring that the engine meets the specific requirements for these conditions without affecting the accuracy of the steady-state calibration.

CS-E.105(b) requires that the engine be subjected to a series of programmed speed-ups and slow-downs to verify the structural integrity of the rotating assembly and the stability of the control system. For a gas turbine engine installed in a fixed-wing aircraft, the throttle must be shifted from the minimum continuous power setting to the maximum continuous power setting, and vice versa, at a rate not exceeding 100 percent of the rated speed change per second. Specifically, the transition from idle to maximum continuous power, and from maximum continuous power to idle, shall be completed within a time interval not exceeding 10 seconds. This rate of change is intended to simulate the most severe transient conditions likely to be encountered in normal operation, ensuring that the engine control system can maintain fuel flow and rotor speed within safe limits without causing excessive thermal or mechanical stress. The qualification run must include at least five such cycles, with the engine operating at the extreme settings for a minimum of 30 seconds at each end of the transition to allow for thermal stabilization.

For turbine engine endurance testing, the thrust or power lever must be moved at a rate that simulates the most severe conditions expected in service. Specifically, during acceleration and deceleration transients, the lever shall be moved from the idle position to the maximum continuous or takeoff power setting, and vice versa, at a constant rate. The time required to traverse the full range of lever travel shall not exceed 1.5 seconds. This rate is intended to represent the fastest credible pilot input during normal and emergency operations. The test schedule shall include a minimum of 100 such full-range transients, with the engine operating at the specified power setting for a minimum of 10 seconds at the end of each movement. The engine must be capable of withstanding these rapid changes in fuel flow and turbine inlet temperature without exceeding the limits specified in the engine type certificate data sheet. Any deviation from this 1.5-second transit time must be justified by the applicant and approved by the Agency, demonstrating that the proposed rate is representative of the intended operational profile.

The supporting case shall demonstrate that the engine meets the requirements of CS-E.10.15, including the time to reach the specified output level. If the time to reach the specified output level exceeds 5 seconds, the supporting case shall address the following:

a. The specific operating conditions, including ambient temperature, pressure, and humidity, under which the wind-up time was evaluated.
b. The rationale for the extended wind-up time, including any design features or control system logic that contribute to the delay.
c. The impact of the extended wind-up time on the engine’s ability to meet the thrust or power requirements during the applicable flight phase, including any potential effects on aircraft performance and safety.
d. Any additional testing or analysis performed to validate the engine’s performance under the extended wind-up conditions, including the results of such testing or analysis.
e. The measures taken to ensure that the extended wind-up time does not adversely affect the engine’s reliability, maintainability, or operability.

The applicant shall provide a detailed justification for any power or thrust response time exceeding 5 seconds. This justification must demonstrate that the engine’s response characteristics are consistent with the intended operational profile and do not compromise flight safety. The analysis shall include a quantitative assessment of the transient response, specifically addressing the time required to reach 90 percent of the commanded power or thrust level. The justification must account for the specific control system architecture, including any intentional delays introduced for stability or component protection, and must demonstrate that these delays do not adversely affect the aircraft’s handling qualities or performance during critical flight phases. Furthermore, the applicant shall provide evidence, such as simulation data or test results, that the engine’s response is predictable and that the flight crew can effectively manage the transient behavior. The justification must also address any potential interactions with the aircraft’s flight control systems and ensure that the engine’s response does not lead to unexpected changes in aircraft attitude or speed.

AMC CS-E.115(b)

1. The engine shall be subjected to a series of start-up tests to demonstrate compliance with the requirements of CS-E.115(b). The test sequence shall include a minimum of three cold starts and three warm starts.

2. A cold start is defined as a start initiated after the engine has been shut down and allowed to cool to ambient temperature, or to a temperature not exceeding 100 °C, for a period of at least 30 minutes. The engine shall be started from a stationary condition.

3. A warm start is defined as a start initiated after the engine has been shut down but before the engine temperature has fallen below 100 °C. The time interval between shutdown and the subsequent start shall not exceed 30 minutes.

4. For each start, the engine shall be accelerated to the maximum continuous power setting and maintained at that setting for a minimum of 10 minutes. The engine shall then be decelerated to idle and shut down.

5. The results of each start shall be recorded, including the time to reach 95 percent of the maximum continuous power setting, the peak exhaust gas temperature, and any abnormal indications. The engine shall demonstrate reliable and consistent start-up characteristics under both cold and warm conditions.

For the purpose of demonstrating compliance with CS-E.100, the engine shall be subjected to a minimum of 100 cold starts and 100 hot starts during the endurance run. A cold start is defined as a start initiated after the engine has been shut down and allowed to cool to ambient temperature, or after a period of at least 30 minutes of shutdown, whichever is later. A hot start is defined as a start initiated after a shutdown period of less than 30 minutes, provided the engine has not been operated for a continuous period exceeding 10 minutes prior to the shutdown. The specific number of starts may be adjusted based on the engine's intended operating profile, provided the total number of starts is sufficient to demonstrate the reliability of the starting system and the durability of the engine components under representative thermal and mechanical stresses. The operator shall document the time, temperature, and conditions of each start to ensure traceability and compliance with the approved test plan.

CS-E.105 Cold-weather light-up.

The engine shall be capable of light-up and acceleration to the rated power or thrust at the minimum ambient temperature specified in the engine data sheet. For the purpose of demonstrating compliance with this requirement, the inlet air temperature shall be at or above the minimum ambient temperature specified in the engine data sheet. It is not permissible to utilize chilled inlet air to artificially lower the inlet temperature below the specified minimum ambient temperature for the purpose of demonstrating cold-weather light-up capability. The demonstration shall be conducted using ambient air conditions that represent the coldest expected operating environment for which the engine is certified. If the ambient temperature is higher than the minimum specified temperature, the engine shall be demonstrated to light up and accelerate under those conditions, but this does not constitute a demonstration of compliance with the cold-weather light-up requirement. The engine manufacturer shall provide data showing that the engine can light up and accelerate to rated power or thrust at the minimum ambient temperature without the use of external heating or chilling of the inlet air, unless otherwise specified in the engine data sheet.

CS-E.105 Cold start.

(a) The engine shall be capable of starting from a cold condition in still air at sea level with an ambient temperature of 15 °C.

(b) For the purpose of demonstrating compliance with CS-E.105(a), the engine shall be allowed to ingest air at the ambient temperature specified in CS-E.105(a). The use of pre-cooled air is not permitted for the initial start attempt. However, if the engine fails to start within the time limits specified in the engine manual, the applicant may employ air conditioning or other means to reduce the inlet air temperature to a minimum of 15 °C for subsequent start attempts, provided that such measures do not alter the fundamental aerodynamic or thermodynamic conditions of the start cycle in a manner that would not be representative of normal operational conditions.

AMC-E.105(b)

The applicant should document the specific ambient conditions, including barometric pressure and humidity, during the cold start demonstration. If air conditioning is utilized after an initial failed attempt, the temperature of the air entering the engine inlet should be monitored and recorded to ensure it does not fall below the specified minimum of 15 °C, thereby maintaining the integrity of the cold start test parameters.

AMC CS-E 33.15(b)(2)

1. For a gas turbine engine with an inlet shield, the requirement to demonstrate that ice accumulation in the area forward of the shield does not adversely affect engine performance or operability may be waived if the following conditions are met:

a. The shield is designed such that the area forward of it is not accessible to the engine airflow under normal operating conditions; and

b. It is demonstrated, by analysis or test, that ice accumulation in the area forward of the shield cannot:

(1) Cause a blockage of the inlet that would result in a reduction of airflow to the engine below the minimum required for stable operation; or

(2) Cause a foreign object damage (FOD) hazard to the engine due to the shedding of ice particles into the engine intake.

2. If the shield is not fixed, or if the engine is equipped with an inlet device that allows airflow to bypass the shield, the waiver is not applicable, and full compliance with CS-E 33.15(b) must be demonstrated.

3. The analysis or test referenced in paragraph 1.b. shall consider the worst-case icing conditions specified in CS-E 33.15(a), including the maximum expected ice accretion rate and the potential for ice shedding under high dynamic pressure conditions.

CS-E.10.15 requires that the engine be capable of operating in the presence of ice. However, compliance with the requirements for ice ingestion is not required for ice that forms on the engine inlet guard or other external structures located upstream of the engine inlet, provided that such ice does not obstruct the airflow into the engine or cause foreign object damage to the engine. Specifically, if the ice accumulation on the inlet guard is such that it does not impinge upon the engine fan or compressor blades, and does not create a hazard to the engine's structural integrity or performance, the engine need not be shown to be compliant with the ice ingestion requirements for that specific ice formation. The applicant must demonstrate that the ice on the inlet guard does not affect the engine's ability to meet the requirements of CS-E.10.15, including the ability to maintain thrust and avoid damage. This exemption applies only to ice that is external to the engine's air intake path and does not enter the engine.

For the purposes of CS-E.10.15, the terms "rapid acceleration" and "rapid deceleration" refer to the transient aerodynamic and mechanical loads imposed on the engine during the ingestion of downpours or hailstones. These conditions are characterized by a sudden change in the relative velocity between the air/hail mixture and the engine intake, resulting in a sharp increase or decrease in the dynamic pressure acting on the fan blades and compressor stages. The engine must be designed to withstand these transient loads without sustaining damage that would compromise structural integrity or lead to uncontrolled engine failure. The specific magnitude and duration of these accelerations and decelerations are to be determined by the applicant, taking into account the maximum expected hailstone size, density, and velocity, as well as the engine's operating envelope. The demonstration of compliance may be achieved through analytical methods, ground-based testing, or flight testing, provided that the methods are shown to be adequate to predict the engine's response to these transient events. The applicant must document the assumptions and limitations of the analysis or test data used to demonstrate compliance with this requirement.

For the purposes of CS-E.10.15, the terms "rapid acceleration" and "rapid deceleration" are defined by specific rate-of-change criteria for engine power or torque. A rapid acceleration is characterized by an increase in engine power or torque at a rate exceeding 50 percent of the maximum rated value per second, or a change in rotational speed of more than 100 revolutions per minute per second, whichever is more severe for the specific engine configuration. Conversely, a rapid deceleration is defined as a decrease in engine power or torque at a rate exceeding 50 percent of the maximum rated value per second, or a reduction in rotational speed of more than 100 revolutions per minute per second. These rates are intended to simulate the most severe transient conditions likely to be encountered during normal operation, including those resulting from sudden changes in load or control input. The engine must be demonstrated to operate satisfactorily, without damage or loss of performance, when subjected to these defined rates of change while exposed to the specified rain and hail conditions. The specific thresholds may be adjusted for particular engine types if justified by analysis and test data, provided the safety of the engine is maintained.

AMC CS-E.100(b)(2)

If it is demonstrated that the bird carcass cannot enter the central gas path during the normal trial, the following procedure shall be applied:

1.  The bird shall be positioned such that its center of mass is aligned with the engine inlet centerline.
2.  The engine shall be operated at the normal trial conditions, specifically at the maximum continuous power setting and the corresponding airspeed.
3.  If the bird is not ingested, the trial shall be repeated with the bird positioned at the maximum and minimum radial positions within the inlet capture area, provided these positions are within the geometric limits of the inlet.
4.  If ingestion is still not achieved, the trial shall be conducted at the maximum continuous power setting and the maximum airspeed for which the engine is certified, or at the maximum airspeed for which the aircraft is certified, whichever is lower.
5.  If the bird is not ingested under these conditions, the requirement is considered met, and no further bird ingestion trials are necessary for that specific configuration. The results shall be documented in the test report, including the specific positions and conditions tested.

AMC CS-E.60(b)(2)

If it is demonstrated that the bird will not reach the core under normal operating conditions, the bird-in-the-core test may be conducted at the maximum engine power setting for which the bird is predicted to reach the core. The test shall be performed with the engine at the maximum power setting, at the maximum altitude at which the bird is predicted to reach the core, and at the maximum airspeed for which the bird is predicted to reach the core. The bird shall be introduced into the engine intake at the maximum airspeed for which the bird is predicted to reach the core. The test shall be conducted with the engine at the maximum power setting, at the maximum altitude at which the bird is predicted to reach the core, and at the maximum airspeed for which the bird is predicted to reach the core. The bird shall be introduced into the engine intake at the maximum airspeed for which the bird is predicted to reach the core. The test shall be conducted with the engine at the maximum power setting, at the maximum altitude at which the bird is predicted to reach the core, and at the maximum airspeed for which the bird is predicted to reach the core.

AMC CS-E.1005(b)(2)

The following details shall be recorded for each aerofoil released during the trial:

1.  The specific aerofoil identification number and its position within the engine assembly.
2.  The mass of each fragment, measured to a precision of 0.1 g.
3.  The maximum dimension of each fragment, measured in millimeters.
4.  The location of impact or containment of each fragment relative to the engine casing or containment liner.
5.  A description of the failure mode, including the point of origin and the direction of ejection.

These records shall be compiled into a test report in accordance with the requirements of CS-E.1005(c). The report shall include a detailed analysis of the debris distribution and shall demonstrate that the engine meets the containment requirements specified in CS-E.1005(a). The data shall be sufficient to allow the certification authority to verify that the engine design provides adequate protection against the release of hazardous debris. The test report shall be submitted to the certification authority as part of the compliance demonstration package.

The applicant shall document the debris generated during the blade-off test, including the quantity, size, and material composition of the fragments. This documentation shall be part of the test report submitted to the Agency. The debris shall be collected and retained by the applicant for a period of at least five years following the completion of the test, unless otherwise agreed with the Agency. The applicant shall ensure that the debris is stored in a manner that prevents contamination of other test articles or equipment. The test report shall include a detailed description of the debris collection method and the storage conditions. The Agency may require the applicant to provide additional information regarding the debris, such as the impact of the debris on the engine's performance or the potential for debris to cause damage to other components. The applicant shall ensure that the debris is disposed of in accordance with applicable environmental regulations.

For a powerplant equipped with a free power turbine, the top twisting-limit clearance is defined as the maximum torque that the power turbine can transmit to the shaft without causing damage to the engine or the attached load. In accordance with CS-E.105, the engine must be capable of withstanding this top twisting-limit clearance for a period of at least 30 seconds. This duration is established to ensure that the engine can tolerate transient overloads that may occur during normal operation, such as sudden changes in load or control system transients, without resulting in structural failure or permanent deformation of the power turbine shaft or associated components. The 30-second requirement allows for a realistic assessment of the engine's ability to handle these transient conditions while maintaining structural integrity. Compliance with this requirement must be demonstrated through testing or analysis, showing that the engine can sustain the specified torque for the required duration without exceeding the allowable stress limits for the materials used in the power turbine shaft and related components.

CS-E.10.10.1 The engine shall be capable of withstanding the maximum over-torque limit for a duration of at least 30 seconds without damage to the engine or its components. The maximum over-torque limit is defined as the maximum torque that the engine can produce without exceeding the maximum allowable stress in the turbine disk or shaft. The engine shall be designed to ensure that the over-torque condition does not result in permanent deformation or failure of any structural component. The manufacturer shall provide data demonstrating that the engine can sustain the maximum over-torque limit for the required duration under the specified operating conditions. The test procedure shall include a detailed description of the test setup, instrumentation, and data acquisition methods. The results of the test shall be documented and submitted to the certification authority for review. The engine shall be inspected for any signs of damage or degradation after the test. If any damage is found, the engine shall be repaired and retested until it meets the requirements of this section. The manufacturer shall also provide a maintenance manual that includes instructions for inspecting and maintaining the engine to ensure that it continues to meet the over-torque requirements throughout its service life.

For powerplants holding a 30-second or 2-minute OEI rating, it must be shown that the engine can withstand the effects of a shaft running at a speed exceeding the maximum continuous operating speed. The demonstration shall be conducted by accelerating the engine to a speed at least 10 percent above the maximum continuous operating speed, as defined in the engine type certificate data sheet, for a duration of at least 30 seconds. During this period, the engine shall be operated at the maximum continuous power setting. It must be demonstrated that no damage occurs to the engine structure, including the shaft, bearings, and associated components, which would preclude continued operation. Furthermore, it must be shown that the engine can be brought to a safe shutdown without further damage. The test shall be repeated on a second engine of the same type to confirm the findings. The results of these tests shall be documented in the engine type certificate data sheet, specifying the maximum allowable overspeed condition and the corresponding time limit for which the engine can operate without sustaining damage that would prevent continued operation.

CS-E 34.15 requires that the engine be designed to prevent overspeed conditions that could result in structural failure. For engines equipped with an overspeed protection system, the applicant must demonstrate that the system functions effectively to limit the engine speed. Specifically, for engines with a rated maximum continuous speed, the overspeed protection system must be shown to prevent the engine from exceeding 110 percent of the rated maximum continuous speed for more than 30 seconds, or 115 percent for more than 2 minutes, under all anticipated operating conditions. This includes verification during the 30-second and 2-minute OEI tests. The demonstration must account for the worst-case combination of ambient conditions, engine configuration, and fuel flow settings. If the overspeed protection system fails, the engine must be capable of withstanding the resulting overspeed without catastrophic failure, provided the overspeed does not exceed 115 percent of the rated maximum continuous speed for more than 2 minutes. The applicant must provide data from ground and flight tests, or equivalent analysis, to substantiate compliance with these limits.

The engine shall be designed to ensure that the rotating assembly remains intact under the following conditions:

(a) For the maximum continuous rating, the engine shall be capable of operating at 105 percent of the maximum continuous speed for a duration of at least 30 seconds.

(b) For the takeoff rating, the engine shall be capable of operating at 105 percent of the maximum takeoff speed for a duration of at least 30 seconds.

(c) For the one-engine-inoperative (OEI) rating, where the duration of operation is less than 2.5 minutes, the engine shall be capable of operating at 105 percent of the maximum OEI speed for a duration of at least 30 seconds.

(d) For the maximum continuous rating, the engine shall be capable of operating at 105 percent of the maximum continuous speed for a duration of at least 30 seconds.

(e) For the takeoff rating, the engine shall be capable of operating at 105 percent of the maximum takeoff speed for a duration of at least 30 seconds.

(f) For the one-engine-inoperative (OEI) rating, where the duration of operation is less than 2.5 minutes, the engine shall be capable of operating at 105 percent of the maximum OEI speed for a duration of at least 30 seconds.

For the purpose of demonstrating that the rotor system will remain intact, the applicant shall demonstrate that the rotor blades and associated components will not separate from the rotor hub under the following conditions:

(a) For the maximum continuous power rating, the rotor shall be subjected to a speed of 105 percent of the maximum allowable rotor speed.

(b) For the one-engine-inoperative (OEI) rating, where the time limit is less than 2.5 minutes, the rotor shall be subjected to a speed of 110 percent of the maximum allowable rotor speed.

The demonstration shall be conducted using a representative rotor assembly, including the hub, blades, and any associated structural components. The test shall be performed in a controlled environment, ensuring that the rotor is accelerated to the specified speed and maintained for a duration sufficient to confirm structural integrity. Any deformation or damage observed during the test shall be evaluated to ensure that it does not compromise the safety of the engine or the aircraft. The results of the test shall be documented and submitted as part of the certification application.

The shaft shall be designed to withstand the combined effects of the steady torque and the alternating torque. The alternating torque component shall be determined by applying a factor of 1.1 to the maximum steady torque, or by using the specific fatigue loading spectrum defined in the engine type certificate data, whichever results in the more severe stress condition. For the purpose of fatigue evaluation, the minimum alternating torque to be superimposed on the mean torque shall not be less than 10 percent of the maximum steady torque, unless a more rigorous analysis based on the specific material properties and the expected service life demonstrates that a lower alternating load is sufficient to ensure a fatigue life of at least 1.5 times the design life. This assessment shall account for stress concentrations at keyways, splines, and other geometric discontinuities, utilizing a stress concentration factor derived from detailed finite element analysis or experimental data. The resulting alternating stress shall be evaluated against the material's fatigue limit, adjusted for the appropriate safety factors and environmental conditions, to ensure that no crack initiation or propagation occurs under the specified loading conditions.

For the purpose of torsional fatigue evaluation, the cyclic torque component shall be determined based on the specific operating conditions of the engine. In the absence of more specific data, the cyclic torque amplitude shall be taken as not less than 10 percent of the maximum continuous torque. This cyclic component is superimposed on the mean torque value corresponding to the steady-state operating condition under evaluation. The resulting total torque, comprising both the mean and cyclic components, shall be used to calculate the alternating and mean stresses at critical locations on the shaft. The fatigue life shall be assessed using the appropriate S-N curve for the material, accounting for the stress concentration factor at the relevant cross-section. Where the engine is designed to operate with significant torque fluctuations, such as during transient acceleration or deceleration, the actual measured or calculated torque variations shall be used to define the cyclic component, provided that the resulting fatigue life meets the requirements of CS-E.2535. The evaluation shall consider the most critical combination of torque and bending moments, ensuring that the cumulative damage does not exceed the allowable limit over the design life of the component.

The worst heat levels of the spinning turbine stage following a loss of its chilling airflow shall be determined by analysis or test. The analysis shall account for the maximum credible heat flux resulting from the loss of all chilling air to the affected stage, considering the engine operating condition that produces the highest metal temperatures. The determination shall include the effects of any subsequent transient conditions, such as a power lever up or a fuel flow increase, that may occur immediately after the loss of chilling air.

Breakdowns of the chilling air system that are not credible under normal operating conditions may be excluded from the analysis. Specifically, failures that require the simultaneous occurrence of multiple independent component failures, or failures that are prevented by the design of the system (e.g., by the use of redundant seals or check valves), may be omitted. However, single-point failures of the chilling air supply duct, seals, or bleed air valves that could result in a total loss of chilling air to the stage must be considered. The analysis shall demonstrate that the turbine stage metal temperatures remain within the limits established in CS-E.10.

For the purpose of determining the maximum turbine rotor temperature, the analysis shall consider the failure of the cooling air supply system. The worst-case condition is defined as the simultaneous occurrence of the most severe credible failures that result in the minimum cooling air flow to the turbine rotor. This includes the failure of the cooling air bleed system, the blockage of cooling air passages, and the failure of the turbine disk cooling air supply. However, the analysis may exclude failures that are not credible, such as the simultaneous failure of all cooling air supply systems, or failures that are mitigated by the design of the engine. The maximum turbine rotor temperature shall be determined by considering the maximum engine power output, the maximum ambient temperature, and the minimum cooling air flow. The analysis shall also consider the effects of the cooling air flow on the turbine rotor temperature, including the effects of the cooling air flow on the turbine rotor stress and the turbine rotor life. The maximum turbine rotor temperature shall be used to determine the turbine rotor material selection and the turbine rotor design.

The maximum continuous rating shall be established by operating the gas turbine at its maximum outlet-gas temperature for a period of at least 30 minutes. This duration is intended to demonstrate that the engine can sustain the specified thrust or power level without exceeding the defined thermal limits. The 30-minute test interval may be divided into two or more separate periods, provided that the total cumulative time equals or exceeds 30 minutes. Each individual period must be of sufficient duration to allow the engine to reach a steady-state condition at the specified operating point. The engine must be operated at the maximum outlet-gas temperature setting throughout each period, and the resulting data shall be used to verify that the engine meets the requirements of CS-E.1005. The division of the test time is permissible only if the engine is allowed to cool to ambient temperature between periods, ensuring that the thermal history of the engine components is representative of normal operational conditions.

The engine must be capable of withstanding the maximum engine gas temperature (EGT) limit for a continuous period of at least 10 minutes without exceeding the specified limits for thrust, fuel flow, or other parameters. This duration is established to demonstrate the engine's ability to operate at the limit under steady-state conditions. The 10-minute run-up may be interrupted for a total duration not exceeding 5 minutes, provided that the engine is not shut down and the EGT does not fall below 90 percent of the limit for more than 1 minute. If the EGT falls below this threshold for a longer period, the 10-minute continuous operation requirement must be restarted. The engine must also demonstrate that it can be shut down and restarted within the limits specified in CS-E.10. The data from this test must be recorded and submitted as part of the type certification application.

For engines equipped with a water injection system, the qualification test procedure shall be modified to account for the effects of ambient temperature on the cooling fluid. When the standard-day lift-off power is restored by the injection of a cooling fluid, the long-duration qualification run shall be conducted at the maximum ambient temperature for which the engine is certified, rather than at standard day conditions. The test shall verify that the engine can maintain the required lift-off power output for the specified duration without exceeding the limits defined in CS-E.250. The cooling fluid flow rate shall be maintained at the maximum value corresponding to the certified ambient temperature. Additionally, the test shall include a check to ensure that the water injection system does not cause any adverse effects on engine components, such as corrosion or erosion, over the duration of the test. The results of this test shall be documented and submitted as part of the type certification data package.

CS-E.105(b) requires that the engine be operated for a period of 10 hours at the maximum continuous power rating. When refrigerant injection is employed to maintain ISA take-off performance under hot-day conditions, the endurance test must be conducted with the refrigerant injection system fully operational. The test shall be performed at the ambient temperature and pressure corresponding to the specific hot-day condition for which the engine is certified, ensuring that the refrigerant flow rate is maintained at the value required to achieve the rated power output. The engine must be operated at the maximum continuous power rating, with the refrigerant injection system active, for the full 10-hour duration. During this period, the engine must meet the performance, emissions, and durability requirements specified in CS-E.105. The refrigerant supply system must be capable of maintaining the required flow rate throughout the test, and any degradation in refrigerant flow or pressure must be monitored and recorded. The test results shall demonstrate that the engine maintains its rated performance and reliability when operating with refrigerant injection under the specified hot-day conditions.

For the purpose of demonstrating compliance with CS-E10.15, the deployment range of the thrust reverser shall be evaluated over the full operational envelope. For a thrust reverser intended for use on the ground only, the deployment range shall be from the stowed position to the fully deployed position, inclusive of any intermediate positions utilized for taxiing or ground deceleration. The trials shall verify that the reverser operates reliably within this ground-specific span, ensuring that the aerodynamic and mechanical loads do not exceed the design limits during the transition from stowed to fully deployed.

For a thrust reverser capable of deployment in flight, the deployment range shall encompass the full operational envelope from the stowed position to the fully deployed position, including all intermediate positions. The evaluation must account for the specific flight conditions, including altitude, Mach number, and engine thrust settings, where the reverser is permitted to operate. The trials shall demonstrate that the reverser maintains structural integrity and functional performance throughout this in-flight deployment span, ensuring that the transition between stowed and deployed configurations does not adversely affect the engine's operability or the aircraft's flight characteristics.

For the purpose of determining the duty cycle of the thrust reverser system, the following assumptions shall be applied to the ground-only deployment duration per cycle. For landing and taxiing operations, the total deployment time shall be assumed to be 10 seconds. This duration encompasses the time required for deceleration on the runway and subsequent taxiing. For in-flight use, where applicable, the deployment time shall be assumed to be 5 seconds per cycle. These values represent the maximum expected continuous deployment times for a single landing event. The thermal and structural loads on the thrust reverser system shall be evaluated based on these assumed deployment durations, ensuring that the system remains within its design limits for both ground and in-flight scenarios. The specific deployment times may be adjusted based on the particular aircraft type and operational profile, but the stated values serve as the baseline for compliance with the relevant structural and thermal requirements.

The stationary-holding brake shall be operated at least three times during the long qualification run. Each operation shall be performed with the propeller rotating at a speed not exceeding 1,000 r/min. The brake shall be applied and released while the propeller is in motion, and the system shall be verified to hold the propeller stationary without damage to the brake mechanism or the propeller hub. The specific speed limit of 1,000 r/min is established to ensure that the kinetic energy involved in the braking event remains within the design limits of the brake assembly, thereby validating the thermal and mechanical integrity of the system under representative operational conditions. This requirement ensures that the brake is capable of safely arresting the propeller rotation during maintenance or emergency scenarios, consistent with the safety objectives of CS-E 900.

CS-E 900.15 requires that the propeller parking brake be applied during the engine run-up procedure. The brake shall be applied when the propeller is rotating at a speed not exceeding 1,000 rpm. The number of applications is not specified as a fixed count; rather, the brake must be applied and released as necessary to verify its function. Specifically, the brake shall be applied at least once during the run-up to confirm that it holds the propeller stationary. The application must be made at a propeller speed of 1,000 rpm or less to ensure safe engagement and to prevent damage to the brake mechanism. The brake must hold the propeller securely in the parked position until released. This requirement ensures that the parking brake is functional and safe for use during ground operations. The engine run-up procedure shall include a check of the parking brake at the specified speed to verify compliance with this provision.

The engine manufacturer shall establish and document the advised operating range for airborne restarts, defining the specific limits within which the engine is certified to restart reliably. This range shall be expressed in terms of ambient temperature, pressure altitude, and Mach number, or equivalent flight conditions. The manufacturer shall specify the minimum and maximum ambient temperatures, the minimum and maximum pressure altitudes, and the minimum and maximum Mach numbers for which the engine is designed to restart. Additionally, the manufacturer shall define the minimum fuel flow required for a successful restart and the maximum allowable engine pressure ratio (EPR) or equivalent parameter at the time of restart. The advised operating range shall be provided in the engine operating manual and shall be clearly indicated to the aircraft manufacturer for incorporation into the aircraft flight manual. The manufacturer shall demonstrate compliance with these limits through testing or analysis, ensuring that the engine can restart within the specified parameters under the conditions of CS-E 33.11. The range shall account for variations in engine condition, including new, average, and worn engines, and shall consider the effects of fuel temperature and humidity where applicable.

AMC CS-E 33.11-1

The air restart envelope shall be defined by the boundary of the region within which the engine is capable of restarting from a windmilling condition. The envelope shall be specified in terms of the following parameters:

a) Ambient static pressure, expressed in kilopascals (kPa);
b) Ambient static temperature, expressed in degrees Celsius (°C);
c) Aircraft true airspeed, expressed in knots (kt); and
d) Engine rotational speed at the moment of ignition, expressed as a percentage of the rated maximum continuous power (RPM).

The boundary of the envelope shall be determined by testing or analysis, demonstrating that the engine can restart within a specified time interval, typically not exceeding 10 seconds, without exceeding the limits specified in CS-E 33.11. The envelope shall be presented as a chart or table, clearly indicating the minimum and maximum values for each parameter. For engines with multiple restart modes, the envelope for each mode shall be defined separately. The data shall be provided in a format suitable for incorporation into the engine flight manual, ensuring that the pilot can readily determine the restart capability under the prevailing atmospheric and flight conditions.

For the purposes of the turbine overheat trial, the term "maximum power-on rotor speed" generally refers to the maximum continuous rotor speed at which the engine is certified for operation under the applicable power setting. However, where the engine is designed to operate at a higher rotor speed for a limited duration, such as during take-off or emergency operation, the momentary rotor speed shall be used in lieu of the maximum continuous rotor speed. This momentary rotor speed is defined as the maximum rotor speed attained during the specific transient condition being evaluated, provided that the duration of operation at this speed does not exceed the limits established in the engine certification data. The trial must be conducted at this momentary rotor speed to ensure that the turbine section is subjected to the thermal and mechanical stresses representative of the most severe operating conditions. The engine manufacturer shall document the specific rotor speed values and the corresponding power settings in the engine manual, clearly distinguishing between continuous and momentary limits to facilitate accurate compliance demonstration.

For the purposes of over-temperature testing, the "maximum power-on rotor speed" is defined as the highest rotational speed at which the engine can operate continuously with the fuel control system in the maximum power-on position, as specified in the engine data sheet. This speed is typically lower than the maximum allowable rotor speed due to the limitations imposed by the fuel control system's maximum fuel flow capability. However, if the engine is equipped with a fuel control system that permits the rotor to accelerate to a speed exceeding the maximum power-on rotor speed during transient conditions, such as during a sudden increase in power demand or a rapid acceleration from idle, the transient rotor speed shall be used for the over-temperature test. In such cases, the test must be conducted at the maximum transient rotor speed, provided that this speed does not exceed the maximum allowable rotor speed specified in the engine data sheet. The objective is to ensure that the turbine components are evaluated under the most severe thermal and mechanical conditions that the engine may experience during normal operation, including transient events.

The powerplant trial supporting the first upkeep schedule must recreate the operating conditions and environmental factors that the powerplant is expected to encounter during its service life. This includes, but is not limited to, the full range of power settings, ambient temperatures, altitudes, and humidity levels specified in the powerplant’s operating envelope. The trial must also simulate the effects of fuel quality variations, including the use of alternative fuels if applicable, and the impact of contaminants such as dust, salt, or ice, as defined in the applicable environmental conditions. Additionally, the trial must account for the cumulative effects of start cycles, idle time, and high-power operation, ensuring that the wear and degradation mechanisms are accurately represented. The data collected from this trial shall be used to establish the initial maintenance intervals and to validate the reliability and durability of the powerplant components. The trial must be conducted in accordance with the approved test procedures and must be documented in a manner that allows for traceability and reproducibility.

The operations-oriented build requirements for gas turbine engines are intended to ensure that the engine is designed, manufactured, and maintained in a manner that supports safe and reliable operation throughout its service life. These requirements focus on the practical aspects of engine installation, maintenance, and repair, ensuring that the engine can be effectively integrated into the aircraft and that its components can be accessed, inspected, and replaced as necessary. The aim is to minimize the risk of in-service failures by addressing potential issues related to engine configuration, component durability, and the availability of spare parts. By emphasizing operational considerations, these requirements help to ensure that the engine meets the performance and reliability standards expected by operators, thereby contributing to the overall safety and efficiency of the aircraft. This approach aligns with the broader objectives of CS-E, which seeks to establish a comprehensive framework for the certification of aircraft engines, taking into account the specific needs and constraints of operational use.

The operational design rules for turbine components are established to ensure that the engine meets the safety objectives defined in CS-E.100. Specifically, these rules are intended to prevent the occurrence of a catastrophic failure that could result in the loss of the aircraft. The design must ensure that any single failure, including the failure of a turbine blade, does not lead to an uncontrolled release of energy or debris that would compromise the structural integrity of the engine or the airframe.

The rules require that the turbine system be designed to withstand the maximum credible operating conditions, including transient events such as engine start, acceleration, and deceleration. The objective is to limit the consequences of a failure to a level that is acceptable for continued safe flight and landing. This is achieved by ensuring that the turbine components have sufficient strength and fatigue life to prevent failure during the service life of the engine, and that any potential failure mode is contained within the engine structure. The design must also account for the effects of foreign object damage (FOD) and other environmental factors that could contribute to component failure.

The powerplant must demonstrate that it meets the requirements of CS-E 1040, which mandates that the engine be capable of operating in accordance with the applicable ETOPS provisions. Specifically, the engine must be designed and evaluated to ensure that the probability of an inoperative engine or a powerplant failure that would result in a loss of thrust is sufficiently low to support the intended ETOPS diversion time. This includes demonstrating compliance with the reliability and maintainability criteria established for the specific engine model, ensuring that the mean time between inoperative events (MTBIE) and the mean time between failures (MTBF) meet the thresholds required for the approved ETOPS range. The evaluation must account for the operational environment, including altitude, temperature, and humidity variations, to confirm that the engine can sustain the required thrust levels and reliability standards throughout the entire ETOPS flight segment.

CS-E 1040 does not prescribe a specific "hit" criterion for ETOPS approval, as ETOPS is an operational approval granted to the aircraft operator by the competent authority, not a direct engine certification requirement. However, CS-E 1040 mandates that the engine must be designed to meet the reliability and maintainability standards necessary to support such operations. Specifically, the engine must demonstrate a mean time between in-flight shutdowns (MTBIS) and a mean time between in-flight containment failures (MTBICF) that satisfy the operational requirements for the intended ETOPS diversion time. The applicant must provide data demonstrating that the engine’s reliability is sufficient to ensure that the probability of an in-flight shutdown or containment failure during a single-engine operation is acceptably low. This is typically achieved through rigorous testing, including the demonstration of containment of failed rotating parts, and by providing statistical data on engine performance. The specific MTBIS and MTBICF values required are determined by the operator’s ETOPS approval and the applicable airworthiness directives, but the engine must be certified to CS-E 1040 to ensure it meets the baseline safety standards for such extended-range operations.

AMC CS-E.1005(b)

1. The following components of a gas turbine engine are susceptible to damage or degradation of performance due to the ingestion of volcanic ash or other eruption cloud particulates:

a) The compressor section, including the fan, low-pressure, and high-pressure compressor stages. Ingestion of abrasive particulates may result in blade erosion, leading to increased tip clearance, reduced aerodynamic efficiency, and potential blade failure.

b) The combustion section, including fuel nozzles, liners, and igniters. Particulate accumulation may cause uneven fuel distribution, hot spots, or blockage of fuel or air passages, potentially leading to unstable combustion or flameout.

c) The turbine section, including the first-stage turbine blades and disks. High-temperature particulates may cause accelerated thermal and mechanical fatigue, blade tip rub, or coating degradation, compromising structural integrity.

d) The exhaust system, including the nozzle and thrust reverser mechanisms. Accumulation of particulates may impede airflow, reduce thrust, or interfere with the operation of moving parts.

2. The applicant shall demonstrate, by analysis, test, or both, that the engine design incorporates adequate protection or mitigation measures to ensure that the ingestion of eruption cloud material, within the limits defined in CS-E.1005(b), does not result in a hazardous condition.

AMC CS-E.1005 Volcanic Cloud Ingestion

1. The following components and systems are susceptible to airworthiness issues resulting from the ingestion of volcanic cloud:

a) Turbine engine hot-section components, including compressor blades, turbine blades, and combustor liners, which may suffer from accelerated erosion, corrosion, or thermal damage due to the presence of abrasive silica particles and corrosive gases.

b) Engine-mounted sensors, such as thermocouples, pressure transducers, and vibration probes, which may experience fouling, blockage, or electrical interference, leading to erroneous indications or loss of signal.

c) Fuel system components, including fuel nozzles and lines, which may become contaminated with particulate matter, potentially causing uneven combustion or clogging.

d) Engine control systems, where particulate ingestion may affect the operation of variable geometry actuators or cause contamination of hydraulic fluid, leading to degraded performance or failure.

e) Exhaust system components, which may experience increased backpressure or structural degradation due to the accumulation of ash deposits.

The operator shall establish procedures to identify and avoid volcanic cloud, and the engine manufacturer shall provide guidance on the effects of volcanic cloud ingestion on engine performance and durability.

The intent of the CS-E specifications regarding thrust reversers is to ensure that the thrust reversal system is designed, installed, and maintained to provide safe and effective operation under all anticipated flight conditions. The specifications require that the thrust reverser system be capable of reversing a sufficient percentage of the engine thrust to meet the required deceleration performance, while also ensuring that the system does not adversely affect the engine's performance, structural integrity, or the aircraft's handling qualities. The design must account for the effects of thrust reversal on the engine's operating limits, including the potential for increased exhaust gas temperatures and the risk of foreign object damage. Furthermore, the specifications mandate that the thrust reverser system be fail-safe, meaning that in the event of a malfunction, the system must either remain in the stowed position or deploy in a manner that does not create a hazardous condition. The intent is to balance the operational benefits of thrust reversal with the safety and reliability of the engine and aircraft system, ensuring that the thrust reverser system contributes to overall flight safety without introducing new risks.

The objective of the power availability procedures is to demonstrate that the engine can provide the required thrust or power within a specified time interval following a defined starting condition, ensuring that the aircraft can meet its performance requirements during critical flight phases. These procedures are designed to verify that the engine’s transient response characteristics, including fuel flow, fuel pressure, and exhaust gas temperature, are within acceptable limits to prevent damage and ensure reliable operation. The procedures must account for variations in ambient conditions, such as temperature, pressure, and humidity, and must be conducted in accordance with the engine’s operating limitations. The results of these tests must show that the engine can achieve the specified power or thrust level within the time limits established by the applicable airworthiness requirements, thereby ensuring that the engine is capable of supporting the aircraft’s performance and safety margins.

The objective of the usage recording system is to provide a reliable, tamper-resistant record of engine operating parameters that are critical for determining the remaining useful life of engine components and for establishing maintenance intervals. This system must accurately capture data such as cycle count, time on wing, and specific operational conditions, including maximum continuous thrust settings and ambient temperature extremes, to support the engine’s life-limited parts management program. The recorded data must be retrievable in a format that allows for the calculation of equivalent cycles or equivalent time, ensuring that the engine’s operational history is traceable and verifiable. By maintaining an accurate log of these parameters, the system facilitates the prediction of component wear and degradation, thereby supporting the safety case for continued airworthiness. The data must be protected against unauthorized modification and must be capable of being downloaded or read out without affecting the normal operation of the engine or its control systems. This ensures that the maintenance provider can make informed decisions regarding the replacement or inspection of life-limited parts, in accordance with the approved maintenance program.

The objective of the bird demonstration required by CS-E 800(a) is to establish that the engine can withstand the ingestion of birds without resulting in uncontained engine failure or damage to the engine that would prevent continued operation. Specifically, the demonstration must show that the engine can ingest birds of a specified mass and velocity, representative of the largest birds likely to be encountered in the operational environment, without causing uncontained engine failure. The demonstration is intended to verify that the engine design provides adequate protection against the effects of bird ingestion, ensuring that the engine can continue to operate safely after the event. The bird demonstration is a critical part of the engine certification process, as it addresses a significant hazard that could affect the safety of the aircraft and its occupants. The demonstration must be conducted in accordance with the procedures and criteria specified in CS-E 800, including the use of birds of a specified mass and velocity, and the evaluation of the engine's performance and structural integrity after the ingestion event.

The overall intent of CS-E 135 is to ensure that the engine is designed and constructed to prevent the release of hazardous quantities of fuel, oil, or other flammable fluids into the engine compartment or the aircraft structure in the event of a failure. This requirement aims to mitigate the risk of fire or explosion by ensuring that any leakage resulting from a failure of a fluid system component, such as a pump, valve, or line, is contained or directed away from ignition sources and critical structural areas. The design must account for the maximum credible flow rates and pressures associated with the specific fluid systems, considering the potential for simultaneous failures where appropriate. Compliance with this provision requires a detailed analysis of all fluid systems, including fuel, hydraulic, and oil systems, to identify potential failure modes that could lead to uncontrolled fluid release. The engine manufacturer must demonstrate, through analysis, test, or both, that the design effectively prevents the accumulation of flammable fluids in areas where they could be ignited, thereby maintaining the safety of the aircraft and its occupants.

The objective of time limited dispatch is to permit the dispatch of an aircraft with a known, non-critical defect or malfunction that does not immediately affect the safe operation of the engine, provided that the defect is identified and documented in accordance with the engine maintenance program. This provision allows for the continuation of flight operations under specific, defined conditions, ensuring that the defect is addressed within a prescribed time limit or flight cycle. The time limit is established based on a risk assessment that considers the nature of the defect, its potential for progression, and the availability of spare parts and maintenance facilities. The objective is to balance operational continuity with safety, ensuring that the defect does not compromise the structural integrity, performance, or reliability of the engine or its components. The time limited dispatch must be approved by the engine manufacturer or an authorized representative, and the specific conditions and limitations must be clearly stated in the dispatch documentation. The objective is to ensure that the defect is rectified before it reaches a state that could affect the safe operation of the engine, thereby maintaining the overall safety of the aircraft and its passengers.

The intent of CS-E 170 is to ensure that the engine is designed to prevent the release of hazardous quantities of fuel, oil, or other flammable fluids into the engine compartment or the aircraft structure in the event of a failure. This requirement aims to mitigate the risk of fire or explosion by containing leaks and preventing the accumulation of combustible materials in areas where ignition sources may be present. The design must account for the failure of individual components, such as seals, gaskets, or fittings, as well as the potential for system overpressure. Compliance is demonstrated by showing that, under the most severe credible failure conditions, the quantity of fluid released is limited to a level that does not pose a significant fire hazard. This includes verifying that any released fluid is directed away from ignition sources and that the engine compartment is designed to prevent the accumulation of vapors. The assessment should consider the operational envelope of the engine, including maximum power settings and altitude conditions, to ensure that the containment measures remain effective throughout the flight.

The intent of the in-service engine evaluation programme is to provide the certification authority with a comprehensive understanding of the engine’s performance, reliability, and maintainability characteristics under actual operating conditions. This programme is designed to verify that the engine meets the requirements of CS-E 25.1 through the systematic collection and analysis of operational data. The evaluation must encompass a statistically significant number of engines operating in a variety of service environments, including different climatic conditions, altitudes, and duty cycles. The data collected shall include, but not be limited to, engine performance parameters, component failure rates, unscheduled maintenance events, and fuel consumption figures. The objective is to identify any potential deficiencies in the engine design, manufacturing processes, or maintenance procedures that could affect safety or airworthiness. The results of this evaluation shall be used to update the engine’s maintenance documentation, service bulletins, and operational limitations as necessary. The programme shall continue until the certification authority is satisfied that the engine’s in-service performance is consistent with the data submitted during the type certification process and that no significant adverse trends are observed.

The intent of the demonstration required by AMC E 740(f)(5) is to verify that the engine’s automatic fire protection system can detect and extinguish a fire within a specified time frame, thereby ensuring that the fire is contained before it can cause catastrophic damage to the engine or airframe. The 30-second limitation is established to provide a conservative margin, accounting for potential delays in fire detection, actuation of extinguishing agents, and the physical process of flame suppression. This time frame is critical for maintaining the structural integrity of the engine and preventing the spread of fire to adjacent components, such as the fuel system or hydraulic lines. By demonstrating compliance with this 30-second criterion, the applicant shows that the fire protection system is effective under realistic operational conditions, including variations in airflow, temperature, and fuel flow. The demonstration must be conducted in accordance with the test procedures outlined in the applicable standards, ensuring that the results are repeatable and representative of actual in-service performance. This requirement supports the overall safety objective of minimizing the risk of fire-related accidents and ensuring that the engine can be safely shut down and isolated in the event of a fire.

CS-E 50, titled "Engine Fire Protection," mandates that the engine fire protection system be designed to detect and extinguish fires within the engine compartment. The system must be capable of detecting a fire in any part of the engine compartment, including the fuel system, oil system, and air intake. Upon detection, the system must automatically initiate the extinguishing process, which typically involves the discharge of fire-extinguishing agent into the engine compartment. The extinguishing agent must be effective against the types of fires likely to occur, such as fuel, oil, and hydraulic fluid fires. The system must also include a means to manually initiate the extinguishing process in the event of a failure of the automatic system. The design must ensure that the fire-extinguishing agent is distributed uniformly throughout the engine compartment to ensure effective fire suppression. Additionally, the system must be designed to prevent the spread of fire to other parts of the aircraft, including the fuselage and wings. The effectiveness of the fire protection system must be demonstrated through testing, including full-scale fire tests, to ensure that it meets the requirements of CS-E 50.

AMC E 560 provides guidance for the compliance with CS-E 560, which requires that the engine be designed to prevent the release of hazardous quantities of fuel, oil, or other fluids in the event of a failure. The acceptable means of compliance involve a detailed analysis of all fluid systems, including fuel, oil, hydraulic, and cooling systems, to identify potential leak paths and failure modes. The analysis must consider the effects of vibration, thermal cycling, and mechanical stress on seals, gaskets, and connections. For each identified failure mode, the engine design must incorporate safeguards, such as redundant seals, leak-off lines, or containment vessels, to ensure that any released fluid is directed away from critical structures and personnel. The compliance demonstration should include test data from engine ground runs and flight tests, showing that under simulated failure conditions, fluid leakage remains within safe limits. Additionally, the maintenance manual must provide clear instructions for inspecting and replacing fluid system components to maintain the integrity of the containment system throughout the engine's service life.

The engine performance data shall be such that the following can be derived and determined:

(a) The engine thrust or power output, as a function of altitude, ambient temperature, and Mach number, for the entire range of operating conditions.

(b) The fuel flow rate, as a function of altitude, ambient temperature, and Mach number, for the entire range of operating conditions.

(c) The engine operating limits, including but not limited to, the maximum and minimum thrust or power settings, and the corresponding engine parameters.

(d) The engine start and restart characteristics, including the minimum ambient temperature and altitude for successful start and restart.

(e) The engine performance degradation with time, as a function of the number of cycles or hours of operation.

(f) The engine performance in the presence of foreign object damage (FOD), as defined in CS-E 20(e)(6).

(g) The engine performance in the presence of icing, as defined in CS-E 20(e)(7).

(h) The engine performance in the presence of water ingestion, as defined in CS-E 20(e)(8).

CS-E 30(b) requires that where an Engine system relies on components outside the Engine type design, the applicant must demonstrate that the Engine system is not adversely affected by the failure or malfunction of those external components. The applicant must identify all such external components and define the specific failure modes or malfunctions that could impact the Engine system. For each identified failure mode, the applicant must show that the Engine system either prevents the failure from occurring, or that the consequences of the failure are acceptable in accordance with the applicable airworthiness requirements. This demonstration must consider the interaction between the Engine system and the external components, including any interfaces, data links, or physical connections. The applicant must provide a detailed analysis, which may include fault tree analysis, failure mode and effects analysis, or other suitable methods, to support the compliance with this requirement. The analysis must be documented and made available to the Agency for review.

The applicant shall declare the ignition system design, including any redundancy provisions, in the engine data sheet. Where the ignition system incorporates redundant channels, the declaration must specify the number of independent ignition channels, the type of redundancy (e.g., dual-channel, triple-channel), and the specific failure modes that the redundancy is designed to mitigate. The declaration shall identify the minimum number of ignition channels required to maintain engine operability under the conditions specified in CS-E 240(a)(1). Furthermore, the applicant must state whether the redundancy is achieved through independent power sources, separate control units, or isolated signal paths, and provide a description of the interlock logic that prevents common-cause failures. This information is necessary to demonstrate compliance with the reliability requirements of CS-E 240 and to allow the certification authority to assess the impact of ignition system failures on engine performance and safety. The declaration must be consistent with the engine maintenance manual and the flight manual, ensuring that operational procedures account for the specific redundancy architecture.

The means of protecting the fuel system from contaminants may be provided in the engine fuel system, the aircraft fuel system, or both. Where the means of protection are provided in the aircraft fuel system, the engine manufacturer shall specify the required level of protection in the engine installation manual. This specification shall include the maximum allowable particle size and concentration, as well as the maximum allowable water content, that the engine fuel system is designed to accept without adverse effect on engine performance or durability. The engine installation manual shall also specify any additional filtration or separation requirements necessary to ensure that the fuel supplied to the engine meets the specified quality standards. The aircraft manufacturer shall ensure that the aircraft fuel system, including any filters or separators, is designed and installed to meet these specified requirements. Compliance with these requirements shall be demonstrated by analysis, test, or both, as appropriate, to ensure that the fuel system protection is effective under all anticipated operating conditions, including those involving the presence of contaminants such as water, particulates, and microbial growth.

The IMP test does not require a fixed number of cycles. The test shall be conducted until the engine reaches a specified condition of damage or failure, or until a predetermined limit of cycles is reached, whichever occurs first. The specific number of cycles, if used as a termination criterion, shall be established by the applicant based on the expected service life and the severity of the test conditions. The test shall be performed at the maximum continuous power rating, or at a lower power rating if specified by the applicant, provided that the lower rating is justified by the expected operational profile. The test shall be conducted in accordance with the procedures outlined in the test plan, which shall include the definition of the test conditions, the monitoring parameters, and the criteria for determining the end of the test.
