For the purpose of demonstrating compliance with the propeller functioning requirements, the engine shall be operated with the propeller control set to the maximum forward pitch position. The propeller control shall then be moved to the minimum forward pitch position, and subsequently returned to the maximum forward pitch position. This sequence constitutes one forward pitch change cycle. A total of ten (10) such cycles shall be performed. During these cycles, the propeller shall be observed to ensure that the blades move smoothly and synchronously through the full range of forward pitch angles without binding, excessive noise, or abnormal vibration. The engine speed shall be maintained within the normal operating range throughout the test. Any indication of mechanical interference, hydraulic leakage, or failure of the propeller to reach the commanded pitch position shall be recorded and investigated. The test shall be conducted at a minimum of two different engine power settings, including the maximum continuous power setting, to verify the propeller's response under varying aerodynamic loads.

For turbine engines equipped with a variable pitch propeller, the propeller functioning tests shall include a demonstration of the propeller control system's ability to maintain the commanded pitch angle under various operating conditions. Specifically, the engine and propeller assembly shall be subjected to a series of forward pitch change cycles to verify the stability and response of the control system. During these tests, the propeller shall be cycled from the minimum forward pitch angle to the maximum forward pitch angle, and back to the minimum forward pitch angle, at a rate not exceeding the maximum rate of pitch change specified by the propeller manufacturer. A minimum of ten (10) such forward pitch change cycles shall be completed. Throughout these cycles, the propeller pitch angle shall remain within the specified tolerance limits, and no abnormal vibrations, noise, or mechanical irregularities shall be observed. The engine operating parameters, including torque, rotational speed, and fuel flow, shall be monitored to ensure they remain within the approved operating envelope. The results of these cycles shall be recorded and evaluated to confirm that the propeller control system functions in accordance with the design specifications and that the propeller blades do not exhibit any signs of fatigue or damage.

For the purpose of vibration testing, the applicant shall declare the specific installation assumptions that define the boundary conditions of the engine. These declarations must include the mass, stiffness, and damping characteristics of the engine mounts, as well as the mass and inertia properties of the attached accessories and exhaust system. The declared values shall represent the most severe conditions expected during normal operation, including the maximum and minimum operating speeds and the corresponding torque loads. Where the engine is designed for multiple installation configurations, the applicant shall identify the specific configuration for which the test is conducted, ensuring that the test setup accurately replicates the declared mass and stiffness parameters. The test rig shall be designed to simulate the declared installation conditions, with particular attention paid to the coupling of the crankshaft and the support of the cylinder block. Any deviations from the declared assumptions must be justified and documented, demonstrating that the resulting vibration levels remain within the limits specified in CS-E.200. The applicant shall provide a detailed description of the test setup, including the location and orientation of accelerometers, to ensure that the measured vibration levels are representative of the actual installation environment.

The applicant shall declare the installation assumptions used for the vibration testing of the engine. These assumptions shall include the specific engine model, the rated power or thrust setting, and the rotational speed. The declared assumptions shall define the boundary conditions applied to the engine during testing, including the method of mounting the engine on the test stand, the location and type of supports, and the constraints applied to the engine structure. The applicant shall specify the mass and stiffness properties of the attached components, such as the exhaust system, intake, and accessory drives, that are assumed to be present during the test. If the test configuration differs from the intended installation, the applicant shall provide a justification demonstrating that the test conditions are conservative with respect to the vibration environment experienced in the intended installation. The declared assumptions shall be documented in the test report and shall be consistent with the data used for the vibration analysis of the engine structure.

CS-E 34.11 Icing of air entering the engine.

The applicant must show that icing of the air entering the engine does not degrade the functioning of the engine. This requirement applies to the engine operating in the normal operating envelope, including at idle speed. The applicant must demonstrate compliance by showing that the engine can operate satisfactorily with ice accumulation on the air intake system, including the air filter, throttle body, and any associated ducting. The demonstration must account for the worst-case ice formation conditions expected during flight, considering the engine's specific air intake design and the potential for ice to restrict airflow or cause mechanical interference. The applicant may use ground tests, flight tests, or a combination of both, supported by analytical methods, to demonstrate that the engine maintains acceptable performance and reliability under these conditions. The analysis must consider the effects of ice on the air-fuel mixture, ignition system, and any sensors or actuators that could be affected by ice accumulation. The applicant must also demonstrate that the engine can be restarted after a period of operation with ice accumulation, if applicable.

The engine shall be designed such that the functioning of the engine is not degraded by icing of the air entering the engine. This requirement applies to the engine operating in the icing conditions specified in CS-E.1005. The design shall ensure that ice formation on the engine inlet, compressor blades, or other critical internal components does not lead to a loss of thrust, a change in engine speed, or a reduction in the margin to surge or stall. Acceptable means of compliance include the use of inlet design features that minimize ice ingestion, such as lip radii and inlet geometry, and the provision of anti-ice or de-ice systems for the engine inlet and compressor stages. The effectiveness of these measures shall be demonstrated through analysis, ground testing, or flight testing, as appropriate, to show that the engine meets the performance and safety criteria under the specified icing conditions. The engine manufacturer shall provide data demonstrating that the engine can operate safely within the certified envelope, including the icing conditions, without exceeding the limits specified in CS-E.1005.

For engines with cylinders and a crankshaft, the rain certification demonstration shall be conducted by exposing the engine to a water spray at a rate of 25 mm per hour. This rate is equivalent to a flow of 25 liters per square meter per hour. The water shall be applied uniformly over the engine assembly, including the air intake system, while the engine is operating at its maximum continuous power rating. The demonstration shall continue for a minimum of 30 minutes, or until the engine fails to meet the applicable performance and emissions requirements, whichever occurs first. The water temperature shall be maintained between 15 °C and 25 °C. The engine shall be considered to have passed the rain certification if it continues to operate within the specified limits without evidence of water ingestion into the combustion chambers or lubrication system, and without any degradation in performance or increase in emissions beyond the limits specified in CS-E.2605.

For the purpose of demonstrating compliance with CS-E.10.15, the rain certification demonstration shall be conducted using a water flow rate of 25.4 mm per hour (1.0 inch per hour). This rate is defined as the amount of water falling vertically onto a horizontal surface in one hour. The water shall be applied to the engine in a manner that simulates natural rainfall, ensuring that the water is distributed uniformly over the engine intake and external surfaces. The demonstration shall be performed with the engine operating at the maximum continuous power or thrust setting, or at a lower power setting if specified by the engine manufacturer, provided that the lower setting is representative of the most critical operating condition for water ingestion. The water temperature shall be maintained at a minimum of 10 °C (50 °F) to prevent freezing within the engine system during the test. The engine shall be operated for a minimum of 30 minutes under these conditions, and no damage, performance degradation, or operational anomalies shall be observed that would compromise the safety of the aircraft.

CS-E 10.15 requires that the engine be grounded to the main engine earth to minimize the consequences of charge accumulation, specifically: (a) electrical shock to personnel; (b) ignition of flammable vapors; and (c) damage to electronic components. To demonstrate compliance, the applicant must provide a bonding analysis showing that all modules and accessories are bonded to the main engine earth. This may be achieved by: (1) providing a detailed wiring diagram and bonding schedule identifying all bonding points and their resistance values; (2) conducting a physical inspection to verify the presence and integrity of bonding straps, lugs, or conductive fasteners; and (3) performing a continuity test on the installed engine, demonstrating that the resistance between any accessible metallic part and the main engine earth terminal does not exceed 0.1 ohms. The bonding scheme must account for thermal expansion, vibration, and corrosion, ensuring a continuous low-impedance path throughout the engine's service life.

For the purpose of certification tests, the fuel used shall be a representative fuel of the type for which the engine is intended, or a fuel of equivalent or higher quality. The oil used shall be of the type and grade specified by the engine manufacturer for normal operation. When a test represents maximum continuous power at altitude, the applicant is permitted to use a fuel with a Research Octane Number (RON) up to 5 points higher than the fuel specified for normal operation, provided that the engine is designed to operate satisfactorily on the lower octane fuel. This latitude is intended to account for the reduced knock tendency at altitude due to lower manifold pressure and temperature. The specific fuel and oil characteristics, including viscosity and additive packages, must be documented in the test report. The engine must demonstrate compliance with all applicable performance and emission requirements using these specified fluids. Any deviation from the standard fuel specification must be justified by the applicant and accepted by the Authority.

For engine systems or components where the other certification tests cannot adequately substantiate compliance, additional tests or analyses shall be performed. These additional tests or analyses must demonstrate that the engine system or component meets the applicable requirements of this Specification. The applicant is expected to define the scope and nature of these additional tests or analyses. In doing so, the applicant shall pay particular attention to the specific failure modes, operational envelopes, and environmental conditions that are not fully covered by the standard test procedures. The definition of the work shall ensure that the additional data provides a high degree of confidence in the safety and reliability of the system or component under all anticipated operating conditions. The Administrator may require specific test conditions or analytical methods to be included in the additional test program to ensure adequate substantiation.

For piston engines equipped with variable pitch propellers, the propeller functioning tests shall include a minimum of three reverse pitch change cycles. Each cycle shall consist of a transition from the maximum declared forward pitch to the maximum declared reverse pitch, and subsequently back to the maximum declared forward pitch. During these cycles, the engine shall be operated at the maximum declared power setting for a duration of at least 30 seconds in the reverse pitch position. An allowance for cooling is provided such that the engine may be operated at idle speed for a period not exceeding 60 seconds between consecutive cycles to permit the propeller and associated control system to cool. The tests shall be conducted in accordance with the conditions specified in CS-E.10.15, ensuring that the propeller control system maintains the commanded pitch within the specified tolerances throughout the entire duration of the test.

The applicant shall establish and maintain a quality assurance system that ensures the engine and its components are manufactured in accordance with the approved design data. Manufacturing methods and processes shall be controlled to ensure that the resulting product meets the specified requirements for material properties, dimensions, and performance. For critical components, the applicant shall define and document the manufacturing processes, including heat treatment, machining, and inspection procedures, to ensure consistency and traceability.

Forgings shall be classified based on the consequence of failure. Class 1 forgings are those where failure would result in a catastrophic failure of the engine or a hazard to the aircraft. Class 2 forgings are those where failure would result in a major failure of the engine or a significant hazard to the aircraft. Class 3 forgings are those where failure would result in a minor failure of the engine or a negligible hazard to the aircraft. The applicant shall apply appropriate inspection and testing requirements to each class of forging, with Class 1 forgings requiring the most stringent controls, including full volumetric inspection and material certification.

The engine shall be provided with a means to alert the pilot and to record the usage of the 30-Second and 2-Minute OEI ratings. A check of the alerting and recording means shall be provided for the purpose of verifying their operational status. The 30-Second OEI power level shall be considered to be in use when the engine is operating at a power level exceeding the 2-Minute OEI rating, or when the 30-Second OEI rating is specifically selected by the pilot. The recording means shall accumulate the total time the engine operates at the 30-Second OEI rating. The alerting means shall provide a distinct indication to the pilot when the 30-Second OEI rating is being utilized, ensuring that the pilot is aware of the time limitations associated with this rating. The design of the alerting and recording systems shall ensure that they function reliably under all anticipated operating conditions, including those encountered during rotorcraft operations. The maintenance procedures shall include specific instructions for checking the functionality of these systems to ensure continued compliance with the certification requirements.

The applicant must demonstrate that the engine is designed to prevent the occurrence of single and double faults that could result in an unsafe condition. For single faults, it must be shown that the probability of occurrence is less than 10^-4 per flight hour, or that the fault is not credible. For double faults, the applicant must demonstrate that the probability of occurrence is less than 10^-6 per flight hour, or that the fault is not credible. In the analysis, the applicant shall identify all single and double faults that could lead to an unsafe condition. An unsafe condition is defined as a condition that could result in a fatal accident or serious injury to the occupants. Failure effects that are normally treated as unsafe conditions beyond the flight crew's control include uncommanded engine shutdown, uncommanded engine start, uncommanded fuel shutoff, uncommanded ignition, uncommanded propeller feathering, uncommanded propeller unfeathering, uncommanded propeller pitch change, uncommanded propeller overspeed, uncommanded propeller underspeed, uncommanded propeller lock, uncommanded propeller unlock, uncommanded propeller reverse, uncommanded propeller forward, uncommanded propeller stop, uncommanded propeller start, uncommanded propeller feather, uncommanded propeller unfeather, uncommanded propeller pitch up, uncommanded propeller pitch down, uncommanded propeller overspeed, uncommanded propeller underspeed, uncommanded propeller lock, uncommanded propeller unlock, uncommanded propeller reverse, uncommanded propeller forward, uncommanded propeller stop, uncommanded propeller start, uncommanded propeller feather, uncommanded propeller unfeather, uncommanded propeller pitch up, uncommanded propeller pitch down.

For the purpose of substantiating the continued ignition capability of a compression-ignition piston engine, the cetane number of the fuel must be considered. The minimum cetane number for which the engine is certified shall be recorded in the engine data sheet. To demonstrate compliance with the ignition requirements, the engine shall be tested using fuels that represent the expected range of cetane numbers. It is recommended that the tests be conducted using at least two different fuels: one with a cetane number at the lower limit of the certified range, and another with a cetane number at the upper limit. Additionally, a fuel with a cetane number of 45 is recommended for testing to ensure robustness against low-quality fuels. The engine must maintain satisfactory ignition and combustion characteristics, including stable idle and full-power operation, without misfiring or excessive smoke, when using these specified test fuels. The specific cetane numbers of the test fuels used during the certification process shall be documented in the test report.

The performance of the engine shall be corrected to the standard reference conditions specified in ISO 2533:1975, "Standard Atmosphere," or an equivalent standard accepted by the Agency. For piston engines, the reference conditions are defined as a sea-level ambient temperature of 15 °C, a barometric pressure of 101.325 kPa, and a relative humidity of 0 percent. When determining the corrected performance, the effects of ambient temperature, pressure, and humidity on the engine's power output, fuel consumption, and exhaust emissions shall be accounted for in accordance with the methods outlined in the applicable standard. The applicant shall demonstrate that the engine meets the required performance levels under these corrected conditions. If the engine is equipped with a supercharger or turbocharger, the correction factors shall be applied to the indicated power or shaft power, as appropriate, to ensure a consistent basis for comparison across different ambient environments. The specific correction formulas and data reduction procedures shall be documented in the engine's type design data package and made available for review during the certification process.

The vibration tests shall be conducted over the range of crankshaft speeds from 50 percent to 115 percent of the maximum continuous power rating, as defined in CS-E1.15. The tests shall be performed at a constant power setting, with the engine operating at the specified speed for a duration sufficient to ensure steady-state conditions. The maximum stress in the crankshaft and propeller shaft system shall be determined by analyzing the combined effects of static and dynamic loads. Static loads include the weight of the rotating assembly and the torque reaction, while dynamic loads are derived from the measured vibration amplitudes. The stress calculation shall account for the first and second critical speeds of the shaft system, ensuring that the operating range does not encompass any critical speed where resonance could occur. The results shall demonstrate that the maximum calculated stress does not exceed 75 percent of the ultimate strength of the material, or 100 percent of the yield strength, whichever is lower, at any point in the shaft system.

The sea-level power calibration curves shall be established prior to the commencement of the endurance test. These curves are required to define the engine’s performance baseline against which power changes during the test are identified. For the purposes of this requirement, the calibration curves shall be determined at the rated speed and at the maximum continuous speed, if different. The curves shall be established using a new or overhauled engine, or an engine that has been subjected to a complete overhaul, to ensure that the baseline performance is representative of a serviceable engine. The calibration data shall be recorded in accordance with the test procedure specified in the applicable test report. The curves shall be used to determine the power output at the beginning and end of the endurance test, and at any intermediate points where a power change is suspected. The power change shall be calculated as the difference between the power output at the end of the test and the power output at the beginning of the test, corrected for ambient conditions. The power change shall not exceed the limits specified in the applicable certification specification.

For piston engines, the low temperature starting test shall be conducted at the lowest ambient temperature for which the engine is certified. The engine shall be started successfully from a cold soak condition at this temperature. The test shall be repeated for a total of three consecutive starts. The oil inlet temperature for each start shall be at or below the lowest oil inlet temperature for which the engine is certified, but not less than -40 °C. The engine shall be capable of starting and reaching the specified minimum running speed within the time limits prescribed in CS-E.10.15. It is recommended that the minimum starting temperature be declared as the lowest ambient temperature at which the engine can be started successfully from a cold soak condition, in accordance with the procedures of CS-E.10.15. This declared temperature shall be used for the determination of the engine’s operating limits and for the provision of information to the aircraft manufacturer. The test results shall demonstrate that the engine meets the requirements of CS-E.10.15 at the declared minimum starting temperature.

The applicant shall declare the specific anti-icing additive type and concentration required for compliance. To demonstrate compliance with the fuel system requirements, the engine must be tested with fuel containing a solid contaminant concentration of 10 mg/litre, with a maximum particle size of 100 micrometres. Additionally, the fuel shall contain a water contamination level of 100 mg/litre, distributed as droplets with a maximum diameter of 100 micrometres. The engine must operate satisfactorily under these conditions without degradation of performance or damage to the fuel system components. The applicant shall provide data demonstrating that the fuel system, including filters and injectors, maintains acceptable flow and pressure characteristics when the fuel is contaminated to these specified levels. The anti-icing additive shall be present at the minimum concentration recommended by the additive manufacturer to ensure effective protection against ice formation in the fuel system. Compliance must be shown for the full range of engine operating conditions, including idle, cruise, and maximum power settings.

CS-E.10.15 Icing.

(a) If icing can occur in the fuel system, it shall be ensured that the fuel system is protected against the effects of icing.

(b) If an additive is relied upon to protect the fuel system against the effects of icing, the following shall be declared in the engine data sheet:

(1) The type of additive;

(2) The minimum concentration of the additive in the fuel required to provide protection; and

(3) The temperature range within which the additive is effective.

(c) The protective means shall be capable of being operated in the following manner:

(1) Automatically, without pilot intervention, under all anticipated icing conditions; or

(2) Manually, by the pilot, in accordance with the procedures specified in the engine data sheet.

AMC CS-E.10.15(b)

The declaration of the additive type, minimum concentration, and effective temperature range shall be based on data obtained from tests conducted in accordance with the applicable icing conditions. The data shall demonstrate that the additive prevents the formation of ice in the fuel system and that any ice formed is removed or rendered harmless. The effective temperature range shall be defined as the range of ambient temperatures within which the additive provides the required protection.

CS-E 34.13 requires that the oil tank be designed to provide adequate expansion space for the oil. The adequacy of this space shall be determined by the engine manufacturer, taking into account the maximum operating temperature and the minimum oil quantity. The venting system for the oil tank and the oil system shall be designed to prevent the accumulation of pressure or vacuum within the tank or system during normal and emergency operating conditions. Specifically, the venting system must ensure that the oil tank does not rupture or leak oil due to internal pressure differentials. Furthermore, the venting system shall be designed to prevent the ingestion of foreign objects and to minimize the risk of fire by directing any expelled oil or vapors away from hot engine components and ignition sources. The design shall also account for the potential for oil mist or vapor generation during high-temperature operation, ensuring that such emissions are managed in a manner that does not compromise the safety of the aircraft or the environment. Compliance with these requirements shall be demonstrated through analysis, testing, or both, as appropriate.

The engine shall be designed to contain debris from compressor or turbine blades, shed singly or in likely combinations, within the engine structure. Containment is required to prevent debris from penetrating the engine casing and causing damage to the aircraft structure or systems that could result in a hazardous failure condition. When evaluating containment, the design shall account for the trajectories of failed blades. Specifically, the analysis must consider off-plane trajectories, including those resulting from blade tip clearance variations, blade-to-blade interactions, and the influence of engine rotation. The containment system shall be capable of withstanding the impact of debris traveling along these off-plane paths, ensuring that no debris penetrates the containment boundary. The evaluation shall include the effects of blade shedding at various engine operating conditions, including maximum continuous power and takeoff power settings. The design shall ensure that the containment system remains effective under the most severe credible failure scenarios, including the simultaneous shedding of multiple blades in a likely combination.

The design shall avoid the occurrence of a catastrophic failure of the engine resulting from the ingestion of foreign matter that is likely to affect only one engine in a flight. For the purposes of this requirement, the following events need not be considered: the ingestion of foreign matter that is likely to affect all engines in a flight; the ingestion of foreign matter that is likely to affect only one engine in a flight, but where the engine is not operating; and the ingestion of foreign matter that is likely to affect only one engine in a flight, but where the engine is not required for continued safe flight and landing. However, the design must account for the ingestion of loose objects, such as cleaning cloths, hand tools, or other similar items, that are likely to be present in the engine intake area during maintenance or servicing. Substantiation of the engine’s ability to withstand the ingestion of such loose objects is required when these objects are likely to be present in the intake area during normal operations or during maintenance activities that could result in their ingestion. The substantiation shall demonstrate that the engine can withstand the ingestion of these objects without resulting in a catastrophic failure.

The static pressure-loaded parts of the engine shall be subjected to a pressure of 1.5 times the maximum working pressure to check for permanent distortion or leakage. For the purpose of this requirement, the maximum working pressure is defined as the highest pressure that can be developed in the system under normal operating conditions, including any transient overpressure conditions that may occur during engine operation. This test shall be conducted with the engine in a static condition, and the pressure shall be applied gradually to avoid shock loading. The parts shall be inspected for any signs of permanent distortion, such as bulging or deformation, and for any leakage at joints, seals, or other potential leak points. The inspection shall be performed using appropriate methods, such as visual examination, pressure decay testing, or leak detection equipment, to ensure that the integrity of the pressure-containing components is maintained. The results of the test shall be recorded and documented in accordance with the engine's maintenance and inspection procedures.

The evidence shall assure that the engine can operate satisfactorily with the fuel system contaminated to the extent that the filtration system is designed to handle. Specifically, the test must demonstrate that the engine maintains satisfactory operation when the fuel system is contaminated with a mixture of water and solid particles, such that the contamination passing through the filtration system does not cause engine damage or loss of thrust. For the complete fuel system test, the engine shall be operated with the fuel system contaminated at a continuous rate of 0.1 percent by volume of water and 0.1 percent by volume of solid particles, unless the engine manufacturer demonstrates that a different rate is appropriate for the specific engine design. The contamination shall be introduced upstream of the fuel filter, and the engine shall be operated at the maximum continuous power setting for a duration sufficient to demonstrate that the engine can tolerate the contamination without adverse effects on performance or structural integrity.

The locking device shall be subjected to a minimum of 100 locking and unlocking cycles. During each cycle, the rotors shall be held in the locked position for a minimum of 10 minutes. The maximum torque assessment shall be conducted with the rotors in the locked position, applying a torque sufficient to attempt rotation of the locked assembly. The device shall demonstrate the ability to maintain the locked state without slippage or failure under this applied torque. The torque value shall be recorded and compared against the design limits specified in the engine manufacturer's data. Any movement exceeding 0.1 degrees during the hold period shall be considered a failure of the locking mechanism. The test shall be performed at ambient temperature and pressure conditions, unless otherwise specified by the engine manufacturer. The results of the torque assessment shall be documented in the test report, including the applied torque, the observed movement, and the final state of the locking device.

CS-E.10.15 requires that the ignition system be designed to ensure reliable engine starting and continuous operation under all anticipated operating conditions. A continuously operated ignition system is necessary to maintain combustion stability during transients, such as rapid changes in thrust, altitude, or ambient temperature, where flameout risk is elevated. This is particularly critical for engines operating in environments with high humidity, rain, or where fuel quality may vary, as the continuous spark prevents flame extinction and ensures smooth power response.

If the substantiation of the ignition system’s performance is conducted on a test rig rather than in an installed engine, the rig must simulate the relevant aerodynamic and thermodynamic conditions of the engine. However, to confirm the durability and reliability of the ignition equipment, including the igniter plugs, leads, and control units, a minimum of 100 hours of engine endurance running is required. This endurance test must be performed on a complete engine, not just the ignition subsystem, to verify that the system operates correctly under the full range of engine operating conditions, including start, idle, cruise, and maximum power settings, without degradation or failure.

For the acceleration demonstration, the engine shall be accelerated from the idle power or thrust level to the maximum continuous power or thrust level. The increase in power or thrust shall be achieved within 10 seconds. If a longer time is required to achieve the specified power or thrust level, the justification for the extended duration shall address the specific operational requirements and the impact on aircraft performance. The demonstration shall be conducted under standard atmospheric conditions, and the engine shall be operated in accordance with the manufacturer's operating procedures. The data collected during the demonstration shall be used to verify that the engine meets the requirements of CS-E.2505. The justification for a longer time shall be documented and submitted to the certification authority for review and approval.

The endurance test shall include a minimum of ten false start attempts. A false start is simulated by introducing a quantity of fuel into the engine that is sufficient to cause a hot start condition, followed by an immediate shutdown of the fuel supply before the engine reaches self-sustaining speed. This procedure is designed to verify the engine’s ability to restart after a fuel-rich condition. Following each false start attempt, the engine shall be allowed to drain for a period of at least 15 minutes. This drainage period is declared to ensure that residual fuel has sufficiently evaporated or drained from the combustor and turbine sections, thereby preventing a subsequent hot start during the subsequent normal start attempt. The normal start following the drainage period shall be conducted in accordance with the manufacturer’s recommended starting procedure, and the engine shall be operated for a minimum of 10 minutes at idle power setting to verify stable operation before proceeding to the next phase of the endurance test.

For the demonstration of acceleration at the declared minimum oil temperature, the control lever shall be moved from the idle position to the maximum continuous power position within 0.5 seconds. The engine shall be allowed to breathe uncooled intake air during this demonstration. The acceleration shall be measured from the point at which the control lever begins to move to the point at which the engine reaches 95 percent of the maximum continuous power. The demonstration shall be conducted with the engine at the declared minimum oil temperature, and the ambient temperature shall be within the range specified in the engine's operating manual. The control lever movement shall be initiated by a single, continuous motion. The engine shall not be subjected to any additional loads or constraints during the acceleration phase. The results of the demonstration shall be recorded and reported in accordance with the applicable data requirements.

For the approval of a maximum over-torque condition on a free power turbine engine, the engine must be demonstrated to operate at the specified over-torque value for a continuous duration of at least 30 seconds. This demonstration must be conducted in runs of a minimum length of 30 seconds, with a minimum of three such runs performed to establish repeatability and stability. Following the completion of these over-torque runs, the engine must be allowed to cool to ambient temperature. Subsequently, the engine must be demonstrated to produce the required One-Engine-Inoperative (OEI) power for a continuous duration of at least 30 seconds, without exceeding the applicable temperature and torque limits. The OEI power must be achieved within the time limits specified in CS-E.33.15, and the engine must maintain this power level for the entire 30-second period. The demonstration must show that the engine can sustain the OEI power requirement immediately after the over-torque event, ensuring that no degradation in performance or structural integrity has occurred.

For turbine engines equipped with thrust reversers intended for ground use only, the certification basis shall include a demonstration of structural integrity and functional reliability under the specific operational constraints defined by the applicant. The test program shall encompass a minimum of 1,000 cycles, each initiated from the typical landing engine speed and accelerated to the declared maximum reverse thrust setting. This cycle count is established to verify the durability of the reversing mechanism, including the actuation system, stator vane tracks, and associated structural components, against the cumulative fatigue loads experienced during normal operational service.

In cases where the thrust reverser is designed exclusively for post-landing braking and taxiing, and not for takeoff or in-flight operation, the sustained duration of maximum reverse thrust application is commonly assumed to be 10 seconds per cycle. This duration reflects the typical time required to decelerate the aircraft from landing speed to a safe taxiing speed, accounting for variations in aircraft weight, runway conditions, and pilot technique. The certification data shall demonstrate that the engine and reverser system can withstand this specific duty cycle without degradation of performance or structural integrity, ensuring that the declared maximum reverse thrust remains available and reliable throughout the service life of the engine.

The operational design specifications for particular aircraft operations, such as ETOPS or time-limited dispatch, are recorded in the engine’s Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS). These specifications set out to determine the engine’s reliability and maintainability characteristics, specifically addressing the probability of in-flight shutdown (IFSD) and the probability of power loss. The TCDS shall identify the specific operational limitations and the associated engine performance data required to support the aircraft’s operational approval. Compliance with these specifications is demonstrated through the engine’s reliability data, maintenance procedures, and the results of the engine’s operational experience. The data shall be sufficient to allow the aircraft manufacturer to establish the operational limits for the specific aircraft type, ensuring that the engine’s performance and reliability meet the requirements for the intended operational environment. The TCDS shall also specify any additional maintenance or inspection requirements necessary to maintain the engine’s reliability within the defined operational limits.

For each dispatchable configuration, it must be shown that the electronic engine control system maintains the ability to control the engine within the limits specified in CS-E.145. Additionally, the system must provide a means to identify the specific fault condition to the flight crew. Under the Minimum Equipment List (MEL) maintenance approach, the maximum operating times for faults are categorized as short time and long time. For an entry-level electronic engine control system, the maximum operating time for a short time fault is typically 30 minutes, while the maximum operating time for a long time fault is generally 10 hours. These values ensure that the engine remains controllable and that the fault is identifiable, allowing for safe operation until the next maintenance opportunity. The specific values may vary based on the engine type and the operator's MEL, but these examples illustrate the regulatory framework for dispatching with electronic engine control system faults present.

Following the completion of the endurance test, the engine shall be operated at the maximum continuous power rating for a minimum of 10 minutes to assess its tendency to backfire. If backfiring occurs, the engine shall be inspected for damage to the intake system, valves, and cylinder head. Subsequently, the engine shall be re-measured to verify that the power output and specific fuel consumption remain within the limits established in CS-E.100. The inspection shall include a visual examination of the intake manifold, air filter, and throttle body for signs of charring or mechanical failure. If any component is found to be damaged, it shall be replaced, and the backfire test shall be repeated until no further backfiring is observed. The final power and fuel consumption measurements shall be taken under standard reference conditions, and the results shall be recorded in the test report. The engine shall be considered to have passed the endurance test only if it meets the power and fuel consumption requirements and exhibits no persistent backfiring after the corrective actions have been implemented.

CS-E.105(b) requires that the engine be capable of operating with the loss of one ignition system. During the endurance test, the loss of one ignition system shall be checked at the maximum continuous power setting. This check shall be performed at the beginning and at the end of the endurance test, and at least once during the test. The power loss resulting from the loss of one ignition system shall not exceed 5 percent of the maximum continuous power. The maximum power loss due to the loss of one ignition system shall be declared in the engine data sheet and the engine operating manual.

For each power calibration curve, the declared temperature may be either the ambient temperature at the time of the test or a corrected temperature, provided the correction is in accordance with the applicable standard. The sea level calibration curves must be established at the beginning of the endurance test, at the end of the endurance test, and at intervals not exceeding 100 hours of operation during the endurance test. These curves shall be determined at sea level, at standard atmospheric conditions, and at the declared temperature. The power output at the declared temperature shall be derived from the sea level calibration curves by applying the appropriate temperature correction factors. The results of the calibration tests shall be recorded and shall demonstrate that the engine meets the declared power ratings throughout the endurance test. Any deviation from the declared power ratings shall be investigated and documented, with corrective actions taken as necessary to ensure compliance with the certification requirements.

Prior to each certification test, all variable devices that are not intended to be adjusted during operation shall be set to the values specified in the engine data sheet or, if not specified, to the values recommended by the engine manufacturer for the specific test condition. These settings shall be verified and recorded prior to the commencement of the test. Following the completion of each test, the settings of these variable devices shall be restored to their original configuration or to the values specified for the subsequent test condition, as applicable. Any deviation from the specified settings shall be documented, and the impact of such deviations on the test results shall be evaluated. The engine manufacturer shall ensure that the settings are consistent with the approved engine data sheet and that any adjustments made are within the limits defined for the engine model. This procedure ensures the repeatability and validity of the certification test data, maintaining compliance with the applicable requirements of this Specification.

Equipment drives not essential to the functioning of the engine shall be disconnected or otherwise rendered inoperative during the calibration tests. The calibration curves shall be established for the engine at all ratings up to and including the maximum continuous rating, as defined in the engine type certificate data sheet. These curves shall relate the engine output, in terms of thrust or shaft power, to the relevant engine parameters, such as fuel flow, turbine inlet temperature, and rotational speed. The calibration process must account for the specific operating conditions, including ambient temperature and pressure, to ensure that the engine performance data accurately reflects the engine's capability across the entire operating envelope. The data obtained from these tests shall be used to define the engine's performance characteristics for certification purposes, ensuring that the engine meets the required standards for safety and efficiency. The calibration curves must be validated through rigorous testing procedures, and any deviations from the expected performance must be investigated and documented.

For time-limited dispatch of a turbine engine with electronic control system faults, each dispatchable configuration must retain the capability for in-flight relight. The constructor’s relight recommendation, as provided in the engine manual, must state the specific altitude and Mach number limits within which relight is assured. This recommendation must account for the degraded performance of the electronic control system and any associated sensor or actuator limitations. The operator must ensure that the engine is operated within these defined limits to maintain compliance with the applicable airworthiness requirements. The relight capability must be verified through analysis or testing, demonstrating that the engine can successfully relight under the specified conditions without exceeding the maximum allowable turbine inlet temperature or other critical parameters. The constructor must provide this information in a format that allows the operator to easily determine the operational envelope for safe relight, ensuring that the engine’s performance and safety margins are maintained throughout the flight.

The design of the rotor-locking device shall ensure that it is capable of locking the rotors in a safe position following an in-flight shutdown, taking into account the infrequent nature of its operation. The device shall be designed to prevent inadvertent release during flight and to withstand the maximum expected loads during engagement. If no means to stop the rotors is fitted, it shall be shown that any continued rotation of the rotors following an in-flight shutdown does not result in a hazardous condition. This demonstration shall consider the effects of continued rotation on the engine structure, surrounding airframe components, and the overall aircraft safety, including the potential for debris generation or structural failure due to centrifugal forces. The analysis shall account for the maximum rotational speed achievable under the specific failure scenario and the duration of continued rotation until the rotors come to a complete stop.

For aeroplane turbine engines controlled manually within their limitations, it must be shown that inadvertent opening of the throttle will not cause the engine to exceed its limitations. This requirement is demonstrated by showing that the engine, when subjected to a full-power throttle command from the minimum power setting, does not exceed the applicable limits for power, torque, or temperature. The demonstration is conducted by applying a full-power throttle input to the engine control system while the engine is operating at idle or minimum power. The resulting engine response is monitored to verify that all parameters remain within the certified limits. If the engine is equipped with a fuel flow limiting device, the demonstration must also confirm that the device functions correctly to prevent fuel flow from exceeding the maximum allowable value. The test conditions must be representative of normal operating conditions, including ambient temperature and pressure variations within the specified range. The results of this demonstration are recorded and reviewed to ensure compliance with the applicable certification specifications.

For the purpose of demonstrating compliance with the requirements for fuel system icing, the applicant shall conduct tests using fuel saturated with water at the lowest anticipated operating temperature. During these tests, a quantity of free water equivalent to 0.1 percent by volume of the fuel shall be dispersed into the saturated fuel. This dispersion simulates the worst-case condition of water contamination resulting from fuel handling and storage. In addition to the steady-state conditions, the applicant must also consider a transient fuel icing condition. This transient condition is defined as the formation of ice crystals in the fuel system due to the rapid cooling of the fuel, which may occur during engine start or during rapid changes in ambient temperature. The applicant shall demonstrate that the fuel system is capable of operating satisfactorily under these transient conditions, ensuring that no blockage of fuel flow or damage to engine components occurs. The testing procedure shall include the monitoring of fuel flow, pressure, and temperature to verify that the system remains within its designed operational limits throughout the transient event.

The engine manufacturer shall provide the aircraft manufacturer with data on the forces and moments transmitted to the engine mountings and airframe structure following a blade failure. This data shall include the peak forces, the duration of the force application, and the direction of the forces, expressed in newtons (N) and newton-metres (Nm). The data shall be derived from tests or analyses that demonstrate the engine’s ability to contain the failed blade and any associated debris within the engine casing or a designated containment area.

It shall be demonstrated that the containment system is effective for the specified blade failure condition, including the release of the blade at the maximum rated speed and the maximum rated temperature. The demonstration shall show that the forces and moments transmitted to the airframe do not exceed the values provided to the aircraft manufacturer, and that the structural integrity of the engine and airframe is maintained. The consequences of the blade failure, including the potential for fire, fume, or fluid leakage, shall be evaluated and shown to be within the limits established by the applicable airworthiness requirements. The data and demonstration results shall be documented in a report that is available to the aircraft manufacturer for integration into the aircraft’s structural design and certification process.

CS-E 33.13 requires that the engine cooling system be monitored to ensure that the engine does not operate in a condition that could result in damage. However, flight crew instrumentation for monitoring the cooling system is not required if the engine is designed such that the cooling system is incapable of failing in a manner that would result in engine damage or a hazardous condition. This exemption is permitted only if the applicant demonstrates, through analysis, test, or both, that the cooling system is inherently safe. The demonstration must show that the system is designed to prevent the engine from operating in a condition that could result in damage, even in the event of a single failure of the cooling system. The evidence must include a detailed analysis of the cooling system's design, including the materials, components, and operating conditions, as well as any relevant test data. The analysis must consider the worst-case scenarios, including the failure of the cooling system's primary and secondary components. The applicant must also demonstrate that the engine's operating limits are such that the engine cannot be operated in a condition that would result in damage, even if the cooling system fails. This demonstration must be documented in the engine's certification data package and must be reviewed and approved by the FAA.

The engine performance and operating limitations shall be determined in accordance with the accuracy of the instruments necessary for controlling the engine. The accuracy of these instruments shall be taken into account in the determination of the engine performance and operating limitations. The engine operating limitations shall be stated in terms of the indications of the instruments necessary for controlling the engine. The instruments necessary for controlling the engine shall be identified in the engine data. The accuracy of the instruments shall be such that the engine operating limitations, when stated in terms of instrument indications, provide a margin of safety. The engine performance data shall be presented in a form that allows the operator to determine the engine performance and operating limitations with the required accuracy. The accuracy of the instruments shall be consistent with the requirements of CS-E. The engine operating limitations shall be clearly defined and shall not be exceeded during normal operation. The instruments necessary for controlling the engine shall be calibrated in accordance with the applicable standards. The accuracy of the instruments shall be verified during the engine certification process. The engine performance and operating limitations shall be documented in the engine manual. The accuracy of the instruments shall be considered in the design of the engine control system. The engine operating limitations shall be based on the worst-case conditions. The accuracy of the instruments shall be sufficient to ensure safe operation of the engine.

The safety assessment of the engine control system shall include an assessment of installation errors. The assessment shall consider the possibility of incorrect wiring, mislabeling of connectors, and improper installation of sensors or actuators. For each identified installation error, the assessment shall determine the resulting system faults and the consequent effects on engine operation. The assessment shall identify any faults that could lead to a hazardous condition, including but not limited to unintended engine shutdown, uncommanded thrust changes, or loss of engine control. Where an installation error could result in a fault that is not detected by the engine control system, the assessment shall evaluate the detectability of the fault by the flight crew and the availability of corrective actions. The assessment shall also consider the impact of installation errors on the reliability of the engine control system and the potential for common cause failures. The results of the assessment shall be documented and shall demonstrate that the probability of a hazardous condition resulting from installation errors is acceptable in accordance with the applicable safety goals.

For piston engines, the failure analysis shall include an assessment of the control system to determine the effects of any failure or malfunction of the control system on the engine. The failure analysis shall establish that no single failure or combination of failures of the control system, which is reasonably likely to occur, will result in a hazardous failure condition. The analysis shall identify all single failures and combinations of failures of the control system that are reasonably likely to occur, and shall demonstrate that the probability of a hazardous failure condition resulting from any such failure or combination of failures is less than 10^-7 per engine hour. Where the control system is part of a larger system, the failure analysis shall consider the interaction between the control system and the rest of the engine. The analysis shall also consider the effects of any failure or malfunction of the control system on the engine's ability to meet the requirements of CS-E. The failure analysis shall be performed in accordance with the methods and criteria specified in AMC 33.1309.

The turbine shaft shall be classified as a critical part. The integrity of the part shall be established by the design assurance system, the production assurance system, and the maintenance assurance system. The design assurance system shall ensure that the part is designed to prevent failure or to contain the failure. The production assurance system shall ensure that the part is manufactured in accordance with the design requirements. The maintenance assurance system shall ensure that the part is maintained in a condition that prevents failure or contains the failure. The classification of the part as critical shall be documented in the design assurance system. The design assurance system shall include a process for identifying critical parts and for ensuring that the integrity of critical parts is established. The production assurance system shall include a process for ensuring that critical parts are manufactured in accordance with the design requirements. The maintenance assurance system shall include a process for ensuring that critical parts are maintained in a condition that prevents failure or contains the failure.

The highest over-speed resulting from a complete loss of load on the turbine rotor may be excluded from the rotor integrity assessment if it is demonstrated that the rotor will not fail due to the stresses associated with that condition. This exclusion is permissible only when the rotor is designed to withstand the maximum operating speed plus the applicable margin, and the transient over-speed does not exceed the limits established for the specific rotor design. In cases where the rotor is not designed to withstand the maximum over-speed, the integrity of the rotor must be assessed for that condition.

Regarding shaft system failures, the probability of failure must be predicted to be less than 10^-7 per engine flight hour. This prediction must be based on a detailed analysis of the shaft system, including the effects of fatigue, creep, and thermal stresses. The analysis must consider all credible failure modes, including those resulting from manufacturing defects, material degradation, and operational stresses. The predicted failure rate must be supported by test data, analytical methods, or a combination of both, and must be validated through a rigorous engineering review. The assessment must ensure that the shaft system is capable of withstanding the maximum expected loads without failure, thereby maintaining the integrity of the engine and ensuring the safety of the aircraft.

For aeroplane turbine engines utilizing refrigerant injection to enhance ISA take-off performance, the 15-minute over-speed test conducted with refrigerant injection shall be performed at a minimum individual run length of 15 minutes. The turbine-entry gas temperature for this specific test condition shall be the maximum turbine-entry gas temperature established for the engine in accordance with CS-E.10, adjusted for the effects of refrigerant injection as determined by the applicant. The test shall be conducted at the maximum continuous power or thrust setting, with the refrigerant injection system operating at its maximum flow rate. The engine shall be operated at the maximum continuous speed, and the turbine-entry gas temperature shall not exceed the limit specified in the engine data sheet for the corresponding power or thrust setting. The test duration shall be continuous, and the engine shall be monitored for any signs of distress or abnormal operation throughout the 15-minute period.

For turbine engines equipped with an integral oil tank, the applicant must demonstrate that the engine can be feathered and that the propeller can be returned to the operating position without the use of external power, following the loss of all available oil down to the feathering reserve. This demonstration shall be conducted under the most unfavorable conditions of altitude, temperature, and engine speed. The feathering reserve shall be a quantity of oil sufficient to permit the propeller to be feathered and returned to the operating position, and shall be trapped in the system such that it is not available for engine lubrication. The minimum quantity of oil trapped for this reserve shall be 0.15 liters (0.04 US gallons) per propeller blade, or as specified by the applicant, provided that the total trapped quantity does not exceed 1.0 liter (0.26 US gallons) for the entire system. The oil level indicator, if provided, shall indicate the presence of this reserve quantity.

The engine shall be designed to tolerate the presence of water and other contaminants in the fuel, in accordance with the limits specified in CS-E.1005. If the engine’s tolerance of fuel contamination relies on the use of an anti-icing additive, the engine shall be certified with the additive included in the fuel system. The specific type, concentration, and operational limitations of the additive shall be declared in the engine data sheet. The details of such assumptions, including the specific additive formulation and the maximum allowable water content, shall be provided in the engine data sheet and the engine manual. The engine data sheet shall specify the conditions under which the additive is required to maintain engine performance and prevent icing. The engine manual shall provide instructions for the use of the additive, including the method of addition, the required concentration, and the frequency of addition. The certification authority shall verify that the engine meets the requirements of CS-E.1005 with the additive present in the fuel system. The engine shall be tested with the additive present in the fuel system to demonstrate compliance with the requirements of CS-E.1005. The test results shall be documented in the engine data sheet and the engine manual.

The engine ETOPS specification is not mandatory for all engine types. Compliance is required only for engines intended to be installed on aircraft certified for Extended Twin-Engine Operational Performance (ETOPS) operations. To be approved for ETOPS capability, the engine must demonstrate that it meets the specific reliability and failure rate requirements defined in CS-E.1450. Specifically, the engine must achieve a mean time between in-flight shutdowns (MTBIS) of no less than 10,000 flight hours, or a failure rate of no more than 0.01 percent per flight hour, for those failures that could result in a complete loss of thrust. This determination must be based on a combination of design analysis, ground testing, and operational data, ensuring that the probability of a dual engine failure or a single engine failure leading to a complete loss of thrust is sufficiently low to support the intended ETOPS dispatch limit. The applicant must provide evidence that the engine’s design, including its fuel system, ignition system, and control systems, incorporates adequate redundancy and fault-tolerant features to meet these stringent reliability criteria.

The airworthiness limitations section of the engine manual shall prescribe the specific maintenance actions required to restore the engine to its continuous rating following the utilization of the 30-second or 2-minute OEI ratings. These actions shall include, but not be limited to, a detailed inspection of the turbine section, a check of the fuel system, and a verification of the engine's performance parameters. The engine manufacturer shall provide the aircraft manufacturer with the necessary data to establish power assurance procedures. This data shall include the maximum allowable time for each OEI rating, the specific conditions under which the ratings may be used, and the precise maintenance actions required to ensure the engine's continued airworthiness. The data shall be presented in a format that allows the aircraft manufacturer to integrate these requirements into the aircraft's maintenance program and operational procedures. The engine manufacturer shall also provide guidance on the monitoring of engine parameters during and after the use of OEI ratings to detect any potential degradation or damage.

The Approved Life of an engine critical part is established to ensure that the part will not fail due to fatigue or other time-dependent mechanisms before the end of its approved life, thereby maintaining the structural integrity and safety of the engine. This information must be included in the Instructions for Continued Airworthiness (ICA) provided to the operator. Specifically, the Approved Life must be clearly identified in the maintenance and inspection procedures section of the ICA. The presentation of this data must be unambiguous, specifying the exact number of cycles, hours, or calendar time, whichever is most restrictive, for which the part is approved. The ICA must explicitly state that the part must be removed from service and replaced or repaired in accordance with the approved data at or before the expiration of its Approved Life. Furthermore, the ICA must detail any specific inspection requirements associated with the part's life limit, ensuring that the operator can readily identify and comply with these mandatory actions to maintain airworthiness.

The safety analysis shall consider the effects of propeller blade pitch control failures, including those resulting from mechanical, hydraulic, or electrical malfunctions, on engine performance and aircraft controllability. The analysis must account for the interaction between propeller thrust, torque, and drag, particularly during critical flight phases such as takeoff, climb, and approach. Hazardous Engine Effects (HEE) are defined as those effects that could lead to a catastrophic failure of the engine or a loss of control of the aircraft. In accordance with the risk assessment methodology, the probability of occurrence of a Hazardous Engine Effect shall be predicted to be less than or equal to 10^-7 per flight hour. This rate ensures that the overall system reliability meets the stringent safety objectives required for the certification of the engine type. The analysis shall also evaluate the consequences of asymmetric thrust and yawing moments resulting from differential propeller blade angles, ensuring that the aircraft remains controllable within the defined flight envelope.

The rotor growth resulting from the over-speed condition shall not cause any damage to the engine mountings. The engine mountings shall be designed to withstand the loads imposed by the rotor during the over-speed condition, including the centrifugal forces generated by the rotating components. These loads shall be evaluated in accordance with the requirements of CS-E.100, considering the maximum credible over-speed condition and the associated dynamic effects. The assessment shall demonstrate that the structural integrity of the mountings is maintained throughout the over-speed event, ensuring that no failure or excessive deformation occurs that could compromise the safety of the aircraft. The design shall account for the combined effects of static and dynamic loads, including any transient forces arising from the rotor dynamics during the over-speed condition.

The requirement for a single large bird ingestion test may be waived if the applicant demonstrates, through analysis or test, that the engine is not susceptible to damage from the ingestion of a single large bird. In such cases, the applicant must provide a blade failure demonstration. This demonstration must show that the engine can withstand the failure of a single fan or compressor blade without resulting in uncontained debris, fire, or explosion. The demonstration must be conducted at the maximum continuous power setting and at the maximum operating speed. The test must verify that the engine remains operable and that no damage occurs to the engine structure or surrounding components that would compromise the safety of the aircraft. The applicant must also demonstrate that the engine can continue to operate at a reduced power setting for a specified period, ensuring that the aircraft can be safely landed. The results of the blade failure demonstration must be documented and submitted to the Agency for review and approval.

The applicant shall demonstrate that the engine can withstand the bird ingestion conditions specified in CS-E.1005 without exceeding the limits established in CS-E.1001. If an engine operating limit is exceeded during the bird ingestion tests, the applicant shall establish that the engine can continue to operate within the limits of CS-E.1001 for a period of time sufficient to allow the aircraft to land safely. Furthermore, the applicant shall establish that the engine can operate within the limits of CS-E.1001 for a period of time sufficient to allow the aircraft to land safely, even if the bird ingestion results in conditions that exceed those substantiated for normal operation. The applicant shall provide data demonstrating that the engine can operate within the limits of CS-E.1001 for a period of time sufficient to allow the aircraft to land safely, and that the engine can be restarted if necessary. The applicant shall also establish that the engine can operate within the limits of CS-E.1001 for a period of time sufficient to allow the aircraft to land safely, even if the bird ingestion results in conditions that exceed those substantiated for normal operation.

CS-E 34.11 Rain and hail.

(a) The applicant must show that the engine can operate satisfactorily in rain and hail. The applicant must demonstrate that the engine can operate satisfactorily in rain and hail at the maximum continuous power or thrust rating, and at the maximum continuous power or thrust rating with the engine operating at the maximum continuous power or thrust rating.

(b) For engines intended for use in aircraft that are certified for operation in rain and hail, the applicant must show that the engine can operate satisfactorily in rain and hail. The applicant must demonstrate that the engine can operate satisfactorily in rain and hail at the maximum continuous power or thrust rating, and at the maximum continuous power or thrust rating with the engine operating at the maximum continuous power or thrust rating.

(c) The applicant must show that the engine can operate satisfactorily in rain and hail. The applicant must demonstrate that the engine can operate satisfactorily in rain and hail at the maximum continuous power or thrust rating, and at the maximum continuous power or thrust rating with the engine operating at the maximum continuous power or thrust rating.

For each engine of the type, the applicant must define the ratings to be tested. During the endurance test, the engine must be operated at the defined ratings. The thrust or power achieved during the test must be at least 95 percent of the rated thrust or power for the specific rating being tested. This requirement applies to all engines of the type for which the applicant seeks certification. The applicant must demonstrate that the engine can maintain the required thrust or power level throughout the duration of the endurance test, accounting for any degradation in performance. The test must be conducted in accordance with the conditions specified in the applicable section of CS-E, ensuring that the engine operates within its approved limits. The data collected during the test must be recorded and analyzed to verify compliance with the specified thrust or power levels. The applicant must provide evidence that the engine meets the required performance criteria for each defined rating, thereby demonstrating the reliability and durability of the engine design.

The approval of jet pipes or propelling nozzles for specific installations is determined by the approval authority based on the results of the endurance test. If the nozzle areas are adjusted to achieve the required test conditions, the justification for these adjustments must be provided to the approval authority. The rating periods of the endurance test must be conducted at the maximum continuous rating temperature, which is defined as the highest temperature at which the engine is certified for continuous operation. This temperature is typically specified in the engine’s type certificate data sheet. The endurance test must be performed with representative exhaust hardware, and any deviations from the standard configuration must be documented and approved. The approval authority will evaluate the impact of any nozzle area adjustments on the engine’s performance and durability, ensuring that the modified configuration meets the requirements of CS-E. The justification must include a detailed analysis of the thermal and mechanical stresses experienced by the exhaust system during the test, demonstrating that the adjusted nozzle areas do not compromise the engine’s safety or reliability.

During turbine endurance test stages conducted with bleed air extraction active, the engine rotational speed may be reduced to maintain the required turbine inlet temperature and to prevent exceeding the maximum allowable rotor stress limits, particularly when the bleed demand significantly alters the engine’s operating point. This reduction ensures that the mechanical integrity of the rotating components is preserved under the specific thermodynamic conditions imposed by the bleed configuration.

When assessing the mean rotational speed for the purpose of demonstrating compliance with the endurance test requirements, these specific stages where the rotational speed is reduced due to bleed operation shall be excluded from the calculation of the mean speed. The mean rotational speed shall be determined based solely on the test stages where the engine is operating at its rated or specified maximum continuous power conditions without the influence of the reduced speed mandated by the bleed configuration. This approach ensures that the endurance test accurately reflects the engine’s performance and durability under normal, full-power operating conditions, while still validating the system’s behavior under bleed extraction scenarios.

The engine and thrust reverser shall comply with the endurance test requirements of CS-E.1005. The endurance test shall be conducted in accordance with the test procedure specified in the applicable AMC. Following the completion of the endurance test, the engine and thrust reverser shall be disassembled and inspected for any damage or wear that could affect the safety of the engine or the thrust reverser. Any damage or wear found shall be evaluated and, if necessary, the engine or thrust reverser shall be repaired or replaced. After any repair or replacement, the engine and thrust reverser shall be reassembled and re-tested to ensure that they meet the requirements of CS-E.1005. The re-test shall include a full inspection and re-measurement of all critical parameters, including thrust, fuel flow, and exhaust gas temperature. The results of the re-test shall be documented and submitted to the certification authority for review and approval.

If an operating limit is exceeded during bird ingestion testing, compliance may be demonstrated by either: (a) showing that the exceedance is within the limits of the engine’s approved transient operating envelope, or (b) demonstrating that the engine can continue to operate within its certified limits following the event without further degradation. For an exhaust gas temperature (EGT) exceedance handled as an approved transient, the engine must be run at the maximum over-temperature for a duration of 30 seconds. This duration is intended to verify that the engine components can withstand the thermal stress associated with the transient condition without resulting in damage that would preclude continued operation within the engine’s certified limits. The test procedure must ensure that the engine is stabilized at the maximum over-temperature condition for the specified time, and subsequent inspection must confirm that no damage has occurred that would affect the engine’s ability to meet the requirements of CS-E.

The engine operating limitations shall include the maximum allowable over-speed condition resulting from inadvertent acceleration. This limitation is defined as the maximum rotational speed that the engine can reach under specific, defined conditions of inadvertent acceleration, such as a sudden loss of load or a malfunction in the fuel control system. The engine must be demonstrated to withstand this over-speed condition without sustaining damage that would preclude continued operation or require immediate shutdown. Specifically, the total duration of running at this maximum over-speed shall not exceed 30 seconds. This demonstration is required to ensure that the engine components, including the rotor system and associated structures, possess sufficient fatigue life and structural integrity to tolerate the transient stress loads associated with such an event. The over-speed limit and the associated time limit shall be clearly stated in the engine operating manual and shall be monitored by the engine control system to prevent exceedance beyond the demonstrated limits.

The applicant shall provide the following information regarding limiter settings for engines with one or more OEI ratings:

(a) The specific limiter settings, including fuel flow, fuel pressure, and any other relevant parameters, for each OEI rating.
(b) The method used to determine these settings, including any test data or analytical methods employed.
(c) The impact of these settings on engine performance, durability, and emissions.

For an engine with a 30-Second OEI rating, the applicant shall ensure that the engine incorporates a means to limit the power output to the specified OEI rating for a duration of 30 seconds. This may include, but is not limited to, the following:

(a) A fuel flow limiter that restricts the fuel flow to the engine to the level corresponding to the 30-Second OEI rating.
(b) A control system that monitors the engine parameters and automatically reduces the power output if the 30-Second OEI rating is exceeded.
(c) A warning system that alerts the pilot if the 30-Second OEI rating is being approached or exceeded.

The applicant shall provide evidence that the engine meets the requirements of this section through testing, analysis, or a combination of both.

Flammable fluid carrying components of a turbine engine may be evaluated to a fire resistant standard, rather than a leak resistant standard, only if the engine is equipped with a means to shut off the supply of flammable fluid to the component. This shut-off means must be capable of stopping the flow of flammable fluid to the component within a time not exceeding 10 seconds after the initiation of the shut-off action.
